full_text:
A change to new offensive coordinator Declan Doyle could help Lamar Jackson and the Ravens offense rediscover its swagger in 2026. Patrick Smith / Getty Images
“The Athletic Football Show” is previewing all 32 teams leading up to the start of the 2026 NFL season. Below are select quotes from the show’s preview of the Baltimore Ravens. The quotes are edited for clarity. You can watch the whole preview on YouTube and in the embedded video below, or listen to the full AFC North preview wherever you get your podcasts.
Robert Mays on what excites him most about the Ravens: I’m excited to see what Jesse Minter can do with some serious dudes. The Chargers have a decent collection of personnel. Derwin James is a good player. Khalil Mack is pretty ageless at this point. Tuli Tuipulotu had a nice season. They have Teair Tart, who they’ve gotten a lot out of, but a lot of the excitement about the Chargers over the last couple of years is their ability to get more than they’ve paid for with some of these guys. The Ravens have invested in some big-name guys all the way across that defense, and I’m excited to see what Minter can do with this level of defensive talent on the high end. Kyle Hamilton. Nate Wiggins. We’ll see what we get from Nnamdi Madubuike. Malaki Starks was a first-round pick. Trey Hendrickson, who they paid a (ton) of money.
I’m interested in not only the overall quality of this, but also how they play. Do they feel like they can play a little bit more man coverage because they have Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey on the outside? Do they get a little bit matchier? The Chargers played two-and-a-half times the amount of quarters that the Ravens played last year. When the Ravens were at their best with this core of pieces two years ago when Mike Macdonald was there, it was these ideas. Even if the system and the language were the same with Zach Orr, stylistically, they had really drifted away from a lot of the stuff that they were doing with Macdonald when this was the best defense in the NFL. And so I think we’ll see them move back in that general direction. And I think with this collection of players and just what we’ve seen from Minter over the last couple of years, it’s a group that’s pretty easy to get excited about.
Dave Helman on what’s keeping him up at night: I’m rooting for him, but Ja’Kobi Lane’s super camp is jumping the shark a little bit. And all of a sudden being excited about a young receiver is doing a lot to distract us from what is otherwise a pretty OK group of pass catchers. I’ve come around on Zay Flowers, I commend the Ravens for getting the deal done early, and I think Zay’s production last year flew under the radar for myself and many others. Even with Zay in the mix, what’s getting you excited about the Ravens pass catchers, unless Lane really is just a rookie phenom? I guess that’s possible, but I wouldn’t bet on it.
Mark Andrews was third on the Ravens roster and 46th in the league among tight ends in yards per route run. That’s down from seventh in 2024 and third the year before that. Behind Andrews, Durham Smythe is going to have a role in what the Ravens want to do. He’s not a pass-catching threat.
Derrik Klassen on what would be a successful season for the 2026 Ravens: I still think that this is a team that should, at worst, get to the divisional round and play a pretty strong game in the divisional round, and I think that they can be even better than that. I still think that this is a really good team and roster. Last year’s disappointment was just that things got a little bit stale and the quarterback was banged up, but I still ultimately think that this is one of the better teams in the NFL.

full_text:
Josh Allen's Bills and Aaron Rodgers' Steelers each have new coaches leading their teams, which makes forecasting their futures challenging. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Thursday’s NFL preseason action .
Change makes things tough to predict. A new coach, a new scheme, a rookie quarterback — all of those changes can have a major impact on how an NFL team performs, and all of them are a challenge for my NFL Projection Model, or any model, to account for.
My model takes into account hundreds of variables, and while taking a data-driven approach is a sound way to make predictions, football is often chaotic and always unpredictable.
Who could have known what Mr. Irrelevant Brock Purdy would become for the San Francisco 49ers? How could one have predicted that then-relatively unknown Sean McVay would turn Jared Goff into an above-average quarterback after a disastrous rookie season?
These are just a couple of examples of how roster decisions and coaching hires can make forecasting the future a challenge.
So, with that background, let’s look at five of the teams that, in my opinion, the model had the hardest time projecting. We’ll start with a couple of teams in the AFC before moving on to the NFC.
Josh Allen is a known commodity, which is a quick way of saying no one and nothing, including my model, doubts the QB will be great in 2026. So why are the Bills on this list? Well, it's the rest of the roster and coaching staff that makes the Bills hard to project.
As it stands right now, the Bills are the model's favorite to win the AFC East (51 percent) and rank atop the AFC when it comes to making the playoffs (74 percent). But with a lackluster receiving group and without many difference-makers on defense, I'm concerned about what happens to this team if Allen sees a dip in production. I love the offensive tackles, and Ed Oliver is great on the defensive front, but outside of that, do the Bills resemble a Super Bowl team? Because that's where they're priced right now, and a scary amount of that optimism rides on the right shoulder and legs of Allen.
They've also handed over the big job to former offensive coordinator Joe Brady. Former coach Sean McDermott may have had his flaws, but Brady is a total unknown as a head coach. I am optimistic about him bringing in Jim Leonhard as defensive coordinator, but he hasn't called plays in the NFL and hasn't called plays at any level since doing so at Wisconsin in 2022.
The Steelers are old, especially on defense and at quarterback, with the soon-to-be 43-year-old Aaron Rodgers under center. As you might imagine, aging curves are also a challenge to predict. We expect players to fall off as they get older, but by how much, and when that starts is tough to forecast.
Will defensive stars like T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey perform at a high level for another season? How far do they drop off? Can they stay healthy?
Beyond age, the most difficult variable to account for is how new coach Mike McCarthy will impact the offense and this roster as a whole. McCarthy probably doesn't belong in the elite tier of coaches, but he is a good one. If he and Rodgers can rekindle some magic from their Green Bay Packers glory days, there is enough talent around them to believe this offense can be above average. Of course, that assumes Rodgers can still handle pressure and hold off Father Time a little longer.
If the older players stay productive and healthy, the Steelers will be in the hunt to defend their AFC North crown. If not, well, there's no Mike Tomlin magic to save the Steelers this season.
Maybe I'm a sucker for believing quarterback Jalen Hurts can return to the level of play he showed during runs to two Super Bowls. If he does, it will likely be because new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion proves to be a big upgrade over his predecessor, Kevin Patullo. But Mannion is an unknown commodity, and he's far from the only question mark on this team.
The Eagles' offensive line isn't the dominant unit it once was, and it's getting up there in the age department. Injuries have become a more persistent problem, and we all saw what happened when star right tackle Lane Johnson, who is 36, went down with an injury last year. There's some noise in these numbers, but with Johnson on the field in 2025, the Eagles offense ranked ninth in adjusted EPA per play; they fell to 26th without him. Is this unit just one injury away from falling off a cliff? We also must acknowledge that longtime offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland is no longer coaching this unit. That kind of change is something a model has a very difficult time quantifying.
The pass rush is also tough to project. Before trading for Jaelan Phillips last year, the Eagles ranked 8th in EPA per play, 21st in success rate and 14th in pressure rate. After acquiring Phillips, those numbers jumped to third, second and third. Phillips is now with the Carolina Panthers, and while the Eagles traded for Jonathan Greenard, his status for Week 1 is up in the air.
Given all of this, are we sure the Eagles are going to win 10-plus games?
My brain is like a ping-pong ball when thinking about the Packers. Sometimes I think they could contend for the Super Bowl; other times I think they'll miss the playoffs. Neither outcome would surprise me.
On one hand, QB Jordan Love and coach Matt LaFleur have produced top-five offenses in two of the past three years, per my model. However, the offensive line is in the worst shape of LaFleur's tenure, and while the pass catchers have tons of potential, wide receiver Christian Watson and Tucker Kraft have concerning injury track records. More injuries could be enough to sink Green Bay's offensive production.
Then there's the defense, where star pass rusher Micah Parsons is out for the first month-plus of the season. Last year, his first in Green Bay, Parsons was a difference-maker for the Packers defense. When Parsons was on the field, the Packers ranked 15th in EPA per play but fell to 28th when he was off the field. That's a stark difference, and it's concerning that even when he was on the field, they were just an average unit.
The last part of the uncertainty for the Packers is their change at defensive coordinator. Jeff Hafley has moved on to coach the Miami Dolphins, and the Packers brought in Jonathan Gannon to replace him. Will Gannon improve the unit? What he gets out of the defense without Parsons on the field could determine the Packers' playoff fate before we reach October.
What are the Giants under new coach John Harbaugh? Are they playoff contenders, or a team that will pick near the top of the 2027 NFL Draft? The play of second-year QB Jaxson Dart will go a long way in determining the answer. He remains a bit of an enigma to project, however, following a promising rookie year filled with injuries.
Combine a perplexing young quarterback with a new scheme and a brand new coaching staff, and you start to see some wide distribution of outcomes.
And then we look at the defense, which has tons of pass rushers. Brian Burns is coming off an awesome season, and the Giants drafted linebacker/pass rusher Arvell Reese at No. 5. But maybe the piece I'm most excited about is pass rusher Abdul Carter. He didn't register the sack numbers last year, but he was incredible at generating pressure. But will this front seven be able to stop the run? After trading defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence to the Cincinnati Bengals, the middle of the defense is thin, and that can lead to these pass rushers being nullified, with the Giants' defense failing to force the offense into true passing situations.

full_text:
Joe Burrow's health is paramount for the Bengals, but they might finally have a defense that can keep up with the offense this season. Megan Briggs / Getty Images
“The Athletic Football Show” is previewing all 32 teams before the start of the 2026 NFL season. Below are select quotes from the show’s preview of the Cincinnati Bengals. The quotes are edited for clarity. You can watch the whole preview on YouTube and in the embedded video below, or listen to the full AFC North preview wherever you get your podcasts.
Robert Mays on what excites him most about the Bengals: I think this is potentially the most complete Bengals offense we have seen. They’ve never finished higher than sixth in EPA per play since Joe Burrow’s been there. Burrow has never finished in the top five in EPA per dropback ever. It’s the sacks. Even in the years they were really good, he’s taking 50 sacks in a season. They’ve always been right on the doorstep of being this overwhelming force. They’ve never quite gotten there because either they’re taking a decent amount of sacks or the run game just doesn’t have the oomph.
Last year, they were a really successful running team in the back half of the season. The offensive line, I think you can make an argument, is as good as it’s been since Burrow got there. You have two homegrown guys that you feel good about among that group for the first time ever, with Dylan Fairchild and Amarius Mims. The run game is higher quality and more consistent. I do think you can get to a place where you can convince yourself this is the best plan and collection of pieces we have seen for this team offensively, even including when they were going to AFC Championship Games and the Super Bowl.
Derrik Klassen on what he’s watching the first month of the season: How much of this offense really is new? How much of it is under center? Are they motioning guys a little bit more? Does the run game add some more stuff to it? When they got under center (last year), they actually could be explosive. When they were a shotgun run team, they really weren’t. They were pretty efficient, but they were not explosive. And when they got under center they had a 9.2 percent explosive run rate, which was top five in the NFL.
Part of that is, I think it was a change-up that teams just weren’t respecting or ready for because they did it at the second-lowest rate in the NFL. Teams that can go under center and run the ball, that is a little bit more of, ‘We are running on our terms and we get to decide how this goes.’ I have a little bit more reservations about their ability to actually get there and tie that into the passing game. I think it’s something that is necessary for them to get over the doorstep from consistently great to elite and actually defining offensive football in the NFL.
Dave Helman on what’s keeping him up at night: I think we’re going to know by Week 2 or Week 3 whether what they did on defense worked. What’s keeping me up at night is that we’ll know in September that it didn’t work and we’re doing the same (thing) all over again, hoping that the Bengals can score their way to the playoffs.
I like Boye Mafe for the contract that he got. I think Bryan Cook is an underrated signing. I even like Kyle Dugger. I thought he did some good stuff for Pittsburgh last year. I don’t think any of this holds up the way that it needs to if Dexter Lawrence isn’t exceptional. Holding him to the 2024 standard before he got hurt is crazy because he was on an unbelievable tear, but he needs to scratch that sort of level if this is going to work at all.

full_text:
The Browns found a potential future star in tight end Harold Fannin Jr. in the 2025 NFL Draft. Gregory Shamus / Getty Images
“The Athletic Football Show” is previewing all 32 teams before the start of the 2026 NFL season. Below are select quotes from the show’s preview of the Cleveland Browns. The quotes are edited for clarity. You can watch the whole preview on YouTube and in the embedded video below, or listen to the full AFC North preview wherever you get your podcasts.
Dave Helman on what excites him most about the Browns: It is probable that last year set my expectations too high. What the Browns did in last year’s draft — you find a future All-Pro-caliber guy in Carson Schwesinger, you redo the tight end room and find a really fun one in Harold Fannin. The running back room is completely revamped; you have two good ones now. Hopefully Mason Graham has more to show you in Year 2. To have all of that from one year, and then you turn around and have two first-round draft picks and a top-40 pick in Denzel Boston, all three of those guys are expected to start. I mean, that’s half your starting lineup in big-time draft picks over the last two years that you have sky-high expectations for. It’s not fair that I’m over the moon about Spencer Fano, KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston mainly because of what the rookie class did last year. If they’re even close to as impactful early as last year’s rookies were, this is an incredibly exciting team by the end of 2026.
Derrik Klassen on what he’s watching the first month of the season: What does the defense look like and how different is it going to be? I think a lot of the front structure and language should be the same. It should be a lot of attacking stuff. I think on passing downs, this thing is going to look a little bit different. Jim Schwartz played a lot more man, and his changeup really was always cover two. The tree that Mike Rutenberg is coming from doesn’t play a lot of cover two. They play a little bit less man and they play a lot more quarters, especially on early downs. If you’re playing it with match principles, it does become man, so that’s more what I expect to see because that’s still how you want to use these corners. That’s still what Denzel Ward does best. That’s still what Tyson Campbell does best. How many growing pains do we get in the first four-to-six weeks where I think every team is really trying to figure out what they want to be and what they want to call?
Robert Mays on what would be a successful season for the 2026 Browns: Is that excitement about the young core maintained throughout the season? When we get to the end of this year, are we in a spot where you’re looking at the collection of guys — (Quinson) Judkins, Schwesinger, Graham, Fannin, Fano, Concepcion, Boston, (Emmanuel) McNeil-Warren — and you’re like, ‘Man, there is a really exciting, promising group of young players here.’ If we find ourselves in a conversation on Dec. 15, being like, ‘You look at the 2027 quarterback carousel and the guys that are going to be available in the draft and the Browns have a top-five pick. Imagine Dante Moore with this group of players. What can this look like?’ If that’s the conversation we’re having after the college football season has wrapped up and we’re transitioning to draft time, that to me is success for the 2026 Browns.

full_text:
Dillon Gabriel (right), who the Browns took in the third round last year, will get a final chance to make an impression on Todd Monken before cutdown day. Ken Blaze / Imagn Images
The Cleveland Browns have made their uninspiring decision regarding their starting quarterback.
By Sunday, they have to determine whether or not to keep four quarterbacks on their 53-man roster. If they choose to only keep three, will they waive second-year passer Dillon Gabriel or rookie sixth-rounder Taylen Green?
Thursday night’s preseason finale will be a showcase game for Gabriel and Green. Green didn’t play at all in the first two preseason games and has taken few full-team reps this summer, with the focus on the competition between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders.
Earlier this week, Browns coach Todd Monken announced Watson as his starter and acknowledged that he long leaned in that direction due to Watson’s seven seasons of NFL experience.
Monken has maintained that he’s not worried about Watson’s reaction to being booed in the Browns’ home stadium last weekend — or that his decision to start Watson doesn’t seem to be popular in Cleveland (or anywhere else). But it’s curious that Sanders, who’s now clearly a backup and a young player who needs more reps, won’t play Thursday night.
None of the starters for the Browns or Patriots are slated to play, but Monken said he’s also sitting Sanders because the team needs to see Gabriel and Green — not because of any potential reaction Sanders might get from the fans while Watson watches from the sideline.
“We’d like to see Dillon more,” Monken said. “(How) it worked out last game, that was unfair to him. So, in order to do that, to see more of him and see Taylen, there’s just not enough reps. …
“Just trying to see Taylen after he played pretty well in the limited reps he had against the Bills (in last week’s joint practice), and we want to see more of Dillon. It just hasn’t worked out trying to get those other guys reps. That’s the reason.”
In any case, Gabriel’s future in Cleveland remains uncertain. He was clearly third in line all offseason, and the team’s long-term quarterback plans seem wide open. Watson is only signed through 2026.
The Browns chose not to add a veteran quarterback in the offseason and drafted Green, believing he was athletic enough to potentially become a long-term developmental option. Green threw a touchdown pass and ran for another in a brief stint in last week’s joint practice, but on most days through camp — including two days of practice this week — Green has only been involved in individual drills.
All 32 teams must trim their rosters to the regular-season size of 53 by Sunday. The first run of the waiver wire will be Monday, at which time teams can officially begin building their 16-man practice squads.
Given the Browns’ ongoing injury issues at tight end and defensive end and the lack of depth across the defense that’s been exposed in the first two preseason games, it seems a certainty that general manager Andrew Berry will be going outside for help in at least two spots at some point between Saturday and early next week.
Though most of the team’s training camp injuries were regarded as minor and linebacker Carson Schwesinger, running back Quinshon Judkins and defensive tackle Maliek Collins returned to practice this week, the Browns lost starting defensive end Alex Wright to a season-ending Achilles injury during last week’s joint practice.
Derek Barnett, the 30-year-old 2017 first-round pick, signed a one-year deal with the Browns and will be in the defensive end rotation.
With Wright out, Isaiah McGuire presumably becomes the starter opposite Jared Verse as McGuire enters the final year of his rookie contract. But the Browns had been actively searching for another player in the edge group before Wright’s injury led them to Barnett, so that’s an area to watch this weekend.
Veteran Julian Okwara and undrafted rookies Khordae Sydnor and Logan Fano are also in the mix, though the Browns moved defensive tackle Mike Hall Jr. to the starting lineup at defensive end for last week’s second preseason game.
Hall is definitely in the team’s plans assuming he can stay healthy. He missed eight games last season while recovering from a knee injury he suffered in the 2024 season finale, and he missed two weeks of this summer’s training camp after he took a hard hit from Judkins in a non-padded practice on Aug. 1.
It’s unlikely that Hall would be a full-time defensive end, but he could earn rotational snaps as the defensive lineups continue to evolve. Given that Barnett was just added and Collins was just activated, the Browns haven’t had their likely opening day defensive line groups in a full practice yet.
Collins’ return from the quad injury that ended his 2025 season came after he spent all of camp on the physically unable to perform list. Collins was seen working out on the field with members of the team’s medical staff during Cleveland’s morning walk-through sessions, and the goal for Collins was to get him back to practice as soon as possible and have him available — and in the starting lineup — for the Sept. 13 season opener.
Defensive tackle Kalia Davis was injured on the first day of training camp and hasn’t practiced since, so it’s impossible to project if he will be on the 53-man roster next week. Collins and Mason Graham will be the starting defensive tackles, with Hall and some combination of Davis, Sam Kamara and Adin Huntington behind them, depending on how the Browns choose to proceed.
For now, let’s consider Thursday night an important audition for young players at all three levels of the Cleveland defense. The Browns have good depth at safety, but it’s hard to say how things will shake out with the roster at cornerback, linebacker and up front.
The Browns have settled on their starting five offensive linemen: Spencer Fano, Zion Johnson, Elgton Jenkins, Teven Jenkins and Tytus Howard. They’re listed from left to right, and they played as a unit in the joint practice with Buffalo . The starting five plus rookie Austin Barber are roster locks.
Rookie center Parker Brailsford is a lock, too, if he’s healthy, but he practiced on Tuesday for the first time in more than three weeks. It’s unclear if Brailsford, who has an injury to his right (snapping) hand, will play Thursday night. But if he returns to health, he’ll be the top backup center.
Either nine or 10 offensive linemen will be on the regular-season roster, which leaves Dawand Jones, KT Leveston, Zak Zinter and Luke Wypler for either two or three spots unless the Browns make an external addition. For most of camp, Leveston played guard but recently has mostly been at tackle, and Barber has repped at right guard. Wypler is a center only, and Zinter could be an emergency center.
With Barber seeming to be next in line at right guard, Jones appears to be a near-lock to make the roster as a backup tackle. If the Browns lost a starting tackle at some point early in the season, they’d choose between Jones and Barber.
Blocking help from the tight end spot figures to be a weekend priority for Berry as other teams shuffle their rosters. Harold Fannin Jr. is the clear No. 1 tight end, with Blake Whiteheart currently the clear No. 2 — and the only other experienced player currently in the group. Rookie Carsen Ryan has mostly worked at fullback, with veteran fullback Michael Burton having been injured for most of August. Burton returned to practice this week.
The Browns lost two blocking tight ends, Jack Stoll and Brenden Bates, to season-ending injuries in August. Rookie tight end Joe Royer missed all of camp for undisclosed personal reasons. Stoll was definitely slated to make the team, and Bates was competing for a spot, so what was once considered a deep area is currently perilously thin.

full_text:
Cowboys third-round pick Jaishawn Barham has shown playmaking ability as a versatile linebacker this preseason. Christian Petersen / Getty Images
FRISCO, Texas — Jaishawn Barham would be just fine with never doing interviews. The Dallas Cowboys rookie linebacker politely declined requests during the entire four-week portion of training camp in California.
He finally took questions from reporters on Tuesday for about three minutes, the first time since rookie minicamp back in May.
Barham just wants to play football. He doesn’t have much interest in talking at great length about himself, but many are interested because of how he has performed on the field. The Cowboys entered the draft with inside linebacker arguably their biggest need. They didn’t select one until Barham in the third round.
He’s now looking like he could be one of the biggest steals of this year’s class.
“He’s awesome,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said. “And I think I’m getting to know Jaishawn on a much closer level. He’s very serious and (has) great intent. You talk about a guy that’s wired the right way. And don’t let his demeanor, the way he carries himself around you guys make you think for one second that he’s not all in for this football team.
“He is very serious at what he does and he wants to be great. But he’s getting more and more comfortable in this locker room around our players and around our coaches. I think he’s a terrific young man.”
The Cowboys don’t do rookie hazing. There’s not even any singing in front of the team.
They do a show where rookies impersonate just about anyone in the organization. One person is off limits: owner and general manager Jerry Jones. During this year’s show, which took place last week, linebacker Langston Patterson was Schottenheimer and first-round pick Caleb Downs was defensive coordinator Christian Parker.
“That’s a good question,” Schottenheimer said. “He was an extra. He was involved. He played his part beautifully. Jaishawn, great job. But he was more of an extra, which some of the guys were only extras.
“He was very good. Oscar-worthy of what he did as an extra.”
Before suffering a groin injury three weeks ago, Barham looked on track to potentially be a Week 1 starter. He missed the first preseason game but returned to practice in time to play in the second one last weekend in Arizona. In 22 defensive snaps, he flashed his impressive athletic ability and aggressive, physical style on several occasions, finishing with multiple QB pressures, a tackle for loss and five total tackles.
“I still got a lot of work to put in,” Barham said. “I’m just trying to get better every day, trusting the coaches, trusting my teammates.”
He shared that he would like to play lower, be better with his hands and improve his sideline-to-sideline coverage in the passing game. He also acknowledged that he’s working to get his conditioning all the way back to where it was before the groin issue.
“All around I’m not perfect,” Barham said, “so there’s a lot of stuff I can still work on.”
The Cowboys were interested in the top available inside linebackers during free agency, but all signed elsewhere. Dallas responded by drafting Barham and then trading for veteran Dee Winters. Those two, combined with DeMarvion Overshown and Shemar James, are at the top of the Cowboys’ depth chart. Overshown and Winters have received the most first-team work in camp.
But Barham has also worked with the first group, including on Tuesday and Wednesday in practices open to fans at The Star. It’s not difficult to envision a playmaking duo of Barham and Overshown. If both stay healthy, it could be exactly what Dallas needs at the linebacker spot to help improve on what was arguably the worst defense in franchise history last season.
“Week 1? I’m ready right now,” Barham said. “For sure. If Week 1 was right now, I’d be ready.”
Barham has the ability to play any linebacker position. He was an off-the-ball linebacker while at Maryland and in his first year at Michigan before moving to edge rusher.
The Athletic ’s Dane Brugler ranked Barham as his 16th overall edge rusher in the 2026 draft class, with a third-to-fourth round grade.
“Barham must improve his discipline and refinement to stay on the field,” Brugler wrote in his ‘The Beast’ draft guide, “but he can create disruption based just on his explosiveness and high activity level. He will need a patient coaching staff ready to cultivate his athletic upside.”
Barham said Tuesday that he believes he has the “perfect coaching staff” in Dallas.
“They’re going to put you in the right spot to make plays,” he added. “It’s up to you to make them.”
Downs and Malachi Lawrence received most of the early attention from this year’s draft class and deservedly so after both were picked in the first round. But the Barham buzz seems to grow every day he’s on the field. He has an intimidating presence whether he’s walking to the locker room or blowing up a run play.
No reason to change what stood out in camp practices carried over into last weekend’s preseason game. But will it be the same when the games count?
“From the time he’s gotten here, we’ve been really excited about the player, the person, the seriousness that he approaches meetings with and the ability to communicate,” Schottenheimer said. “The versatility is real and it kind of goes back to draft day. We did the work, we did the prep, he was there, Jerry made the call, and it was great.”

title: It's Jerry's world, but Stephen Jones could engineer 'a different path' for the Cowboys Zak Keefer 122

full_text:
"I don't have a succession plan," Jerry Jones says about eventually handing off the Dallas Cowboys to his eldest son, Stephen. "One day I just won't be here to toss my two cents in." Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photos: Ronald Martinez, Brooke Sutton / Getty Images
PHOENIX — The call came in the fall of 1988, when he was a reservoir engineer fresh out of college, living in a one-bedroom apartment in Fort Smith, Ark. He spent his days behind the wheel of his Ford pickup, crisscrossing the South, charting oil reserves and piling up profits for his father’s company. The job fit.
“Probably my math mind,” he says.
If he looked hard enough, he could see the next 30 years. He liked that.
Football? He was convinced it was behind him, and he was fine with that. He’d lived his dream. He played at Arkansas, the quarterback recruit who ended up toiling on special teams, starting just one game — his last — and only then because the Razorbacks’ star safety was popped for steroids a few days before Oklahoma smacked them in the Orange Bowl.
A few months later, Dad called and said he wanted to buy the Dallas Cowboys.
“I know you’re starting to find your way in the oil business,” Jerry Jones told his son, “but what do you think about coming to Dallas and learning the football business with me?”
“I’ve already started my car,” Stephen Jones blurted out.
Tucked into a back booth at McArthur’s, the sleek restaurant that sits inside the Arizona Biltmore, the man who will one day run the most valuable sports franchise on the planet is telling the story of the day his life changed.
It’s a Sunday afternoon, late March. The NFL is in town for its annual meetings. Billionaires slip in and out, grabbing lunch before disappearing into conference rooms to debate rule proposals and replacement refs. Stephen Jones, in a white button-down with his collar open and his sleeves rolled back, is in no rush.
“Without that phone call,” he says, “I’d probably still be in the oil business.”
For a moment, the realization seems to surprise him. He never envisioned a different path. He never needed one. He takes a swig of Coke and unleashes a Texas-sized laugh so hearty it envelops half the restaurant. The implication is obvious.
For a 24-year-old, that’s a hell of a job offer.
Dad let him tag along for the first meeting, when Cowboys owner Bum Bright spilled his secret: America’s Team was losing $1 million a month. Within weeks, Bright dropped the price tag from $200 million to $140 million. Stephen held firm. He told his father it was too much.
“Dad’s a dealmaker. Everything he’s ever had his hands on he’s overpaid for,” he says. “I can be a little bit more tightfisted.”
Against his son’s hesitations — plus the advice of his own attorneys and accountants — Jerry put up every dollar he had to buy the team in February 1989, then borrowed the rest at sky-high interest rates. The gamble would come to define his life.
Ambition was innate to Jerry Jones, the need to climb and conquer and rewrite rules along the way. It made him an undeniable American life force, molder of the modern NFL, a man whose aspirations were matched only by his ego. Rarely does he enter a room and not devour the oxygen in it.
If that bothered his oldest son, Stephen never mentioned it. He learned early on he could let Jerry be Jerry and still stand on his own two feet — so long as those feet were a few steps out of frame. They’ve worked together for 37 years now, shoulder-to-shoulder but never quite equal, wrangling over contracts and draft picks and the price of their billion-dollar stadium while building the Cowboys into a commercial colossus. They’re also best friends, fierce loyalists and devoted drinking buddies who never paid much mind to the phrase “last call.”
Jerry and Gene Jones’ younger children are also Cowboys co-owners and executives — daughter Charlotte is chief brand officer and son Jerry Jr. chief sales and marketing officer — but it’s Stephen, 62, whom his father calls “my devil’s advocate” and “my barometer.” His official title: Chief Operating Officer, executive vice president of player personnel and president of AT&T Stadium.
Change is coming. The father relishes risk and the theater that comes with it. The son does not.
“I’m not pushing Jerry out by any means, but when that day comes, it’s gonna feel a lot different,” says Hall of Fame quarterback and Cowboys icon Troy Aikman.
Darren Woodson, another member of the team’s Ring of Honor, is more blunt: “Stephen’s going to chart a different path. He’s got a little bit more motherf—er in him.”
So much of Stephen’s climb is framed through his father. When he was growing up, Jerry would fly from Oklahoma City to Little Rock on weeknights just to coach his YMCA football team. When Stephen reached high school, Jerry rented office space across from the practice field to keep tabs on his progress. “How’d it go today?” Dad would ask each evening, not letting on that he’d spied every snap through a pair of binoculars.
Lessons came in the form of pacts. The dealmaker knew no other way. After Stephen was caught drinking at an eighth-grade school dance, Jerry drove him straight to Arkansas’ War Memorial Stadium. “So, you wanna be a college athlete?” he asked. Stephen nodded. “Then you can’t be a party boy.”
Next came the offer. Tell you what, Stephen, I’ll make a deal with you.
“Your job every day in the summer is to work out for football season,” Jerry told him. “Your ass better be outta the house by 8 a.m., and if I catch you back here before 2 …”
“So you can imagine the look on my dad’s face the next summer when he caught me having a few friends over to the pool one day,” Stephen says.
“Get your suit on!” Jerry barked. “You’ve got an interview.”
They drove in silence, pulled into a Wendy’s parking lot and walked in to meet the manager, who told Stephen he’d start by cleaning bathrooms, dishes and the grease trap before moving on to cooking burgers and fries.
“Can you be here tomorrow at 4 o’clock?” the manager asked.
“Congratulations, you’ve got your first job,” Jerry told his son. “You fired up?”
They walked to the car in silence. Stephen hung his head. His father looked over and asked him if he remembered their deal.
“Well, I’ll tell you what. I told the manager you probably wouldn’t take the job this time, but one more f— up on your part and your ass is gonna be in here every day.”
“I made sure my ass wasn’t back in that house before 2 p.m. ever again!”
He grew into a star quarterback with grades good enough to get into Princeton. That’s where Jerry wanted him to go, and Stephen was all but sold during a campus tour after he heard a young actress named Brooke Shields would be in his freshman class.
Then Arkansas coach Lou Holtz called and offered a scholarship. Arkansas is where Jerry had played, co-captaining the 1964 national championship team as a sub-200-pound right guard, and where Gene had cradled Stephen in her arms on the sideline. It’s where he’d fallen for the game.
“All I’ve ever wanted to do is play ball for the Razorbacks,” he told his parents.
Tell you what, Stephen, I’ll make a deal with you.
“If you go to Arkansas,” Jerry said, “I want you taking the hardest curriculum the school has to offer.”
Stephen graduated as the Razorbacks’ only four-year letterwinner with a degree in chemical engineering. Jerry sneaked into the stadium to watch practices. He also learned something about his son he’d never forget: “If Stephen tells me he’s gonna do something, well, he’s gonna do it.”
Stephen ditched the oil business, moved to Dallas and heeded his father’s advice. He started from the bottom. He was a gofer, a sales rep, an understudy. He learned how to brand the Cowboys and how to sell the Cowboys. He learned to negotiate. “No one’s gonna care about our money like we will,” Jerry used to tell him. He’d fume when his father was criticized in the newspapers, which, back then, was all the time.
He became a buffer, smoothing over some of…

full_text:
The Lions like their defensive front and their options at defensive end opposite star pass-rusher Aidan Hutchinson. Paul Barnick / Imagn Images
It’s hard not to think about it when you’re watching them. The contrasting skill sets, the controlled chaos, the relentless pursuit. You’re so accustomed to what this has been, you almost pause at the idea of what it could be.
What we’re seeing from the Detroit Lions’ defensive line might be real. They need it to be.
“I think all of those guys are just going to elevate each other’s games,” coach Dan Campbell said of his D-line. “I like where we’re at.”
As the regular season nears, a unit that’s historically been a weakness is looking like a strength. Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams are at the forefront of a group that believes it’s built to win in the trenches, in ways we haven’t previously seen.
When Hutchinson was on the board at No. 2 in the 2022 NFL Draft, Lions GM Brad Holmes could hardly contain himself. A homegrown, face-of-the-franchise talent at a major position of need had fallen into his lap. Since then, Hutchinson has grown into the star player the Lions never doubted he’d become.
The only problem has been finding him a complementary partner.
Former starting edge Romeo Okwara, with a 10-sack season two years before Hutchinson arrived, wasn’t the same player after a torn Achilles. Charles Harris, following a 7.5-sack season in 2021, never matched his production in 2022 and 2023. James Houston had a special run as a rookie (eight sacks in seven games), but was a liability against the run and never repeated those totals in Detroit. Marcus Davenport was signed and re-signed to be the power edge the Lions envisioned opposite Hutchinson, but finished with more IR stints (two) than sacks (1.5) over the 2024 and 2025 seasons.
The most productive edge rusher Hutchinson has played with in his career — statistically speaking — is Al-Quadin Muhammad. Signed to be a reserve rush end, Muhammad was forced into the starting lineup after Davenport injured his pec last season. He recorded 11 sacks rushing opposite Hutchinson — the type of pass-rush production that should be applauded, if not for what was sacrificed versus the run.
When Muhammad was on the field last season, the Lions allowed 4.8 yards per rush, per TruMedia, which would’ve ranked 27th. Detroit’s defensive rushing success rate of 58 percent when Muhammad was on the field would’ve ranked 23rd among teams last season. It fell to 53.8 percent in the second half of the season (Weeks 10-18), which would’ve ranked 31st. Muhammad, 31, signed with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this offseason. It felt like the Lions needed to move on from him.
With that, the Lions were back to square one this offseason. Before free agency and the draft, Campbell, Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard and Detroit’s defensive staff sat down and watched every snap of the 2025 season. Where were they susceptible to explosive plays? What was viewed as a player error? Were the coaches putting their guys in the best positions to succeed? What would be their focus for the 2026 season?
“What we’ve done is we’re tearing off all the Band-Aids, trying to look through every crack, crevice to see where the good things were, the bad things were, and where can we improve as coaches, players in totality,” Sheppard said.
One of those conclusions, based on what the Lions added this offseason, was improving the pass rush without sacrificing in the run game. The Lions needed players who could not only win a rush, but set a physical edge and contain the pocket. They believe they have the horses to do so now.
The Lions have been rotating their defensive line at higher rates than we’ve seen under Campbell. It feels like there’s intent behind the madness. Guys aren’t just coming off the field because they need a breather — this staff is mixing and matching.
Tyler Lacy, a post-cutdown roster addition a year ago, has been a mainstay with the first-team defense. Known for his size and length, Lacy profiles as an early-down/run-package option. He can play big end or kick inside to rush, offering the Lions versatility. He has had a full offseason in the system and will be relied upon to do the dirty work for this defensive line.
Veteran DJ Wonnum signed with the Lions this offseason after spending the 2025 season with the Carolina Panthers. Wonnum says this is arguably the best he’s ever felt in training camp. He’s healthy, hungry and he sees the opportunity in front of him, rushing opposite of an elite edge like Hutchinson. The last time he did that, he was in Minnesota with Danielle Hunter — recording a pair of eight-sack seasons in four years, while being a plus against the run.
“We love where Wonnum’s at right now, man,” Campbell said. “He’s another one of these guys. He’s a smart football player. He’s crafty. He knows how to use his length. He’s got a couple of different rushes that are a little bit of a problem and plays the run.”
“I put it on tape early in my career,” Wonnum said. “I’ma go do that this year and prove to myself, prove to my coaches, that I’m a dog.”
And then there’s rookie second-rounder Derrick Moore — a player with all the tools to develop into a long-term answer along this defensive line. Moore has a little bit of everything in his bag. Speed to power, length, versatility to rush inside or on the edge, a motor that stays hot and a developing pass-rush repertoire that should only get better with age. He’s displayed it this preseason, and has been a sub-package rusher with the first-team defense since returning from a groin injury. He’s got the goods to make an impact this year.
“Dating back to the spring, ever since we drafted and acquired Derrick Moore, since the day he showed up, he just has the presence of an older guy,” Sheppard said. “Just being around him, he doesn’t feel like a rookie. I kind of say that to the staff all the time. He’s very mature. He’s kind of introverted, but once you get to know him, he’s just a man’s man and he just comes to work every day with his head down. ‘Coach, what do you need of me? What are you expecting of me? What is the standard?’ And he goes out and tries to meet that.”
On any given play, you could see Hutchinson and Wonnum, Hutchinson and Moore, Hutchinson and Lacy, Lacy and Wonnum, Lacy and Moore, you name it. With more seasoning, Ahmed Hassanein and his relentless motor could join this rotation. Then there’s the defensive tackle room.
McNeill said he feels like himself again after working his way back from a torn ACL. He was playing at a Pro Bowl level two years ago, and his teammates say it’s night and day in terms of where he was last year and this year. Williams, a 2025 first-round pick, has shown promise as a disruptive nose tackle. He’s been excellent against the run, and his power is impressive. After showing up to camp heavier than he’d like, he dropped 50 pounds and banked some trust from Campbell. Elsewhere, Levi Onwuzurike returns from a torn ACL, sixth-round pick Skyler Gill-Howard has been the talk of camp as a three-tech with serious juice, and a vet like Chris Smith or Ben Stille could round out the room for extra depth.
“I feel really good with where our D-line is at right now,” Campbell said. “I feel that group of guys, plus bench. I feel really good, man. I feel like it’s a good group. It’s a versatile group. There’s depth in there. There’s pieces. You can ask them to do different jobs. … I feel really good about it.”
Because the Lions will be without starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, there’s pressure on this defensive line to produce. There’s too much talent, and too much depth, for things not to come together. It hasn’t been a strength historically, but when evaluating how the Lions are going to get it done defensively this year, it all starts up front.

full_text:
Josh Jacobs runs through a drill during training camp. Tork Mason / Imagn Images
Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs will face two criminal charges related to an alleged domestic abuse incident on May 23, the Brown County (Wis.) District Attorney’s Office announced Thursday.
After a months-long investigation, the district attorney ultimately decided to pursue two misdemeanor charges against Jacobs: battery and criminal damage to property.
Jacobs was initially arrested by the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department on May 26 on five charges relating to domestic abuse — felony strangulation and suffocation, and four misdemeanors: battery (domestic abuse), criminal damage to property (domestic abuse), disorderly conduct (domestic abuse) and intimidation of a victim.
Jacobs was jailed but released the following day before appearing virtually in court after the district attorney’s office found insufficient evidence at the time to pursue criminal charges. The D.A.’s office also announced then that it would continue investigating Jacobs since it had reason to believe additional evidence existed that might change what/if any criminal charges were ultimately filed. With that step being taken, Jacobs and the Packers now await potential discipline from the NFL that would sideline him this season.
Outside of the day he was released from jail, Jacobs has participated in every practice this offseason and preseason when healthy since the alleged incident. He missed almost two weeks earlier in training camp with a groin issue.
“We’ve talked internally,” starting quarterback Jordan Love said about Jacobs’ situation in early June. “Everyone knows what the situation is there and we’ve talked, but obviously, the details — everybody’s keeping that under wraps right now just out of respect for the situation and obviously all the legal stuff that’s gonna be playing out. But it’s great to have Josh here with us , being able to work with us and get back to work. … I was shocked when I saw it, and like I said, it’s one of those things, we’re going to let it play out. There’s a lot of uncertainty when you hear something like that of what might happen.”
Jacobs, whom the Packers signed to a four-year, $48 million contract in March 2024, received the backing of Love, other teammates and his head coach, Matt LaFleur. Jacobs has rushed for 2,258 yards and 28 touchdowns in two seasons with the Packers and was voted by teammates as one of the offense’s three season-long captains last season.
“Josh has been great,” LaFleur said in early June. “He’s been great. It’s been great to have him around. He shows up every day with the same attitude, same mentality. I would expect nothing other than that.”
If Jacobs is suspended to start the season, third-year running back MarShawn Lloyd would become the starter and that position would suddenly be a major concern. Jacobs is a true feature back, but Lloyd has played in just one game over two seasons due to a litany of injuries. He has, however, participated in every practice of training camp, but it’ll be a tall task to remain healthy through actual games until Jacobs returns if the Packers keep their top running back.

full_text:
Jonnu Smith was released by the Steelers after one season in Pittsburgh. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
Veteran tight end Jonnu Smith has agreed to a free-agent deal with the Green Bay Packers, a team source confirmed to The Athletic on Thursday. The source spoke on the condition of anonymity because they didn’t have permission to comment publicly.
Smith has spent the past four seasons on four different teams, including the 2025 season with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
Smith was a third-round draft pick of the Tennessee Titans in 2017 and spent his first four seasons there. He signed with the New England Patriots in 2021 and played two years under Bill Belichick before being traded to the Atlanta Falcons. After one year in Atlanta, Smith signed a two-year deal with the Miami Dolphins in 2024 but was traded to the Steelers last offseason.
The Packers are thin on proven options at tight end. Tucker Kraft appears to be fully healthy after rehabbing his torn ACL and is their No. 1. Their No. 2, Luke Musgrave, suffered a neck injury this offseason and hasn’t practiced yet in camp. They also have Josh Whyle, Drake Dabney and Messiah Swinson at the position, but Whyle might be the only one the Packers trust to play significant meaningful snaps in the regular season, and even he doesn’t seem to be much of a threat.
Smith has experience with Packers coach Matt LaFleur, who coached him as the Titans’ offensive coordinator in 2018.
Smith, 31, has been a supplemental part of the passing game for most of his nine-year NFL career. He had one outlier season in 2024, when he set career highs with the Dolphins, catching 88 passes for 884 yards and eight touchdowns. That marks the only time Smith has had more than 50 catches or at least 600 receiving yards in a season.
Smith’s 2025 season was expected to produce better results, because the Steelers’ offensive coordinator was Arthur Smith, who was Smith’s position coach with the Titans and the head coach in Atlanta during Smith’s year with the Falcons. However, the Steelers ended up having more of a tight end-by-committee season, and Smith had just 38 catches for 222 yards and two touchdowns in 17 games.

The Indianapolis Colts haven’t won the AFC South since 2014, winning 10 or more games just once since (2018). Their hopes after an 8-2 start to last season were quickly dashed after a couple one-score losses in Weeks 12 and 13 were followed by losing Daniel Jones to a torn Achilles in Week 14, losing out to finish 8-9.
Now with Jones back, do the Colts have a chance to hang with the Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars in the hunt for the division crown and playoffs?
Their +380 odds at DraftKings give them around a 20 percent implied probability to pull it off. Let’s take a look at the full division, then dive into projections and analysis from my model.
It could be a very close race in the AFC South, especially with Texans wide receiver Jayden Higgins now sidelined for the season with a torn ACL. Their offensive line has already limited their offensive production in recent seasons, so how much of a step forward can the offense really take with limited receiving options? Their defense is elite, which keeps their floor quite high, but I’m not confident enough in their offense to run away with the division.
The Jaguars will have a floor as high as the Texans, just in a more balanced way. I have more confidence in Jacksonville’s offense — a top-10 unit after trading for Jakobi Meyers last year — and its defense is pretty stout, if not to the level of Houston.
The Texans and Jaguars are close when it comes to their chances of taking the division crown. I start to have trouble believing with the third team down.
Yes, the Colts jumped out to a scorching hot start on offense last season before an Achilles injury to Jones derailed their momentum. I’m a big Shane Steichen fan and believe the offense will be in a fine position, but what if Jones takes some time to find his groove or isn’t quite firing on all cylinders? That’s without questioning whether his breakout in Year 7, which is pretty rare for a quarterback, was a fluke or not.
If their offense does take a step back, is the defense good enough to keep them on pace with the Texans and Jaguars? It’s possible, but I’m not quite seeing it right now. There are good duos on the defensive line (DeForest Buckner and Laiatu Latu) and at cornerback (Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward), but the rest of the unit is full of unproven players or question marks.
It’s tight in the AFC South, that’s for sure. But for me, it’s tight between the Texans and Jaguars. The Colts can certainly enter the conversation, but as everything stands right now, I can’t put the Colts in the same tier.

full_text:
Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Alec Pierce signed a four-year, $114 million deal in March — the richest free-agent contract for a receiver in NFL history. Trevor Ruszkowski / Imagn Images
INDIANAPOLIS — The Indianapolis Colts removed wide receiver Alec Pierce from the physically unable to perform list Thursday, allowing him to practice in a limited capacity for the first time this offseason. Before Thursday, Pierce hadn’t taken part in an on-field team activity since undergoing left ankle and heel surgery in late March.
Pierce reiterated Thursday what’s been the team’s message since the spring: He’s hopeful to be on the field for the season opener Sept. 13 against the Baltimore Ravens.
“Week 1 is the goal,” Pierce said after a practice in which he only participated in individual drills.
“First time being back out here, wearing a helmet, playing with other NFL players, you gotta knock a little bit of rust off. But (I’ve) been working in (physical therapy), been working kind of off and on with trainers. They’ve been doing a good job preparing me, getting me ready. Just a little different once you get back out here, get timing from Daniel (Jones) and these other NFL arms.”
Another catch from #Colts WR Alec Pierce in his first practice since undergoing left ankle/heel surgery in March.
(This is a warmup before anyone starts any nonsense about him not running full speed.) pic.twitter.com/PVlRlJ19A6
— James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) August 27, 2026
While the physical rehab has been going well, Pierce said the mental part of it has been challenging.
“It is tough,” said Pierce, who is not expected to play in the Colts’ preseason finale Saturday. “You just gotta find ways to try and stay in it. … It’s good to be around the guys. They keep your spirits up and stuff because sitting and watching film and watching walkthrough, watching practice, it gets a little monotonous. You want to be out there.”
Pierce initially tried to avoid surgery at the end of last season, opting for a platelet-rich plasma injection instead. However, when that injection didn’t alleviate the discomfort, which Pierce said he’d been managing since the 2024 season, he eventually moved forward with a procedure. Pierce revealed in June that he faced a four- to six-month recovery timeline that could threaten his availability for the start of the season.
The fifth-year pro signed a four-year, $114 million deal in March, the richest free-agent contract for a receiver in NFL history. Pierce, who is the league’s 15th-highest-paid wideout annually, has led the NFL in yards per reception in each of the past two years (22.3 in 2024 and 21.3 in 2025).
Pierce is poised to take over as Indy’s No. 1 receiver after the team traded veteran Michael Pittman Jr. to the Pittsburgh Steelers in March. Pittman led the Colts in catches in four of the past five years. In Pittman’s absence, the Colts’ starting receiver trio will consist of Pierce, Josh Downs and, most likely, Keenan Allen . Allen, a six-time Pro Bowler, reached a one-year agreement with the Colts last week.
Shane Steichen acknowledged it will take time for Pierce to play like himself again, but the Colts coach was thrilled to have Pierce back out on the field Thursday.
“Anytime you have a star player come back off an injury and be out there with the guys, it brings a lot of juice to the football team, both sides of the ball,” Steichen said. “It’s great to have him back.”

full_text:
The two-time NFL MVP and three-time Super Bowl champion is coming back from a knee injury. Jamie Squire / Getty Images
The NFL’s incumbent dynasty is at a crossroads.
Last year was the Kansas City Chiefs’ first season without at least a conference championship berth since 2017, back when Alex Smith was under center. The Patrick Mahomes era produced three Super Bowl titles and two more Super Bowl appearances between 2018-24. We’re about to find out if the juice is still fresh in Arrowhead.
Mahomes, who turns 31 years old in September, is coming off a torn ACL and LCL . Travis Kelce, who turns 37 in October, has settled down into married life. Andy Reid now stands as the league’s oldest head coach. Oh, how time passes.
A few notable reinforcements have come to Chiefs Kingdom. Kenneth Walker III, the reigning Super Bowl MVP, arrives to take pressure off of Mahomes and the passing game. Mansoor Delane, the No. 6 pick in April’s draft, could make an instant impact at cornerback. And there are some familiar faces returning as well. Eric Bieniemy is here for a second stint as offensive coordinator. L’Jarius Sneed is back in the secondary, bolstering a defense that still has the likes of Chris Jones, George Karlaftis and Nick Bolton.
Kansas City is currently slated for six primetime appearances, including a Thanksgiving night game, this season. Consider this the one-stop guide to all 17 regular-season broadcasts. Make sure you’re following the Chiefs on The Athletic, too. Jesse Newell , a Kansas native, is one of the best on the beat.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. The Chiefs’ Thanksgiving clash with the Buffalo Bills is also under the “Sunday Night Football” brand … on a Thursday night. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN — including Kansas City’s two MNF appearances — while the other seven are exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17.  The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. All-time Chiefs great Tony Gonzalez is one of the analysts for pregame, halftime and postgame segments. He’s No. 2 in career receiving yards for the franchise.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.

The Los Angeles Rams aren’t done with Tutu Atwell after all. They have acquired their former wide receiver in a trade with the Miami Dolphins in exchange for running back Jarquez Hunter, the team announced on Thursday.
The Rams are bringing back a receiver they drafted in the second round in 2021 who spent the past five seasons with the team. Atwell was a steady producer from 2022 to 2024, catching 99 passes for 1,343 yards and four touchdowns, and Los Angeles re-signed him last offseason to a one-year, $10 million deal.
However, Atwell fell out of the rotation quickly and finished with just six catches for 192 yards and a touchdown on 15 targets. He was often a healthy scratch down the stretch of the season as the Rams leaned into three-tight end sets and had to fix their special teams units on the fly — and Atwell didn’t contribute to that phase.
But now, the Rams are bringing Atwell back. They feel better about their special teams numbers and are still searching for a dependable No. 3 receiver behind Puka Nacua and Davante Adams.
Hunter was a fourth-round pick in 2025, but he was pushed out of playing time by the steady presence of Kyren Williams and Blake Corum, as well as Ronnie Rivers, who contributes on special teams.
The Rams will take on $1.075 million of Atwell’s contract for this season, marking a difference of nearly $9 million from what they paid him last year. They will incur a cap hit of around $250,000 from Hunter’s deal as part of the trade.
The Rams are now likely to keep just three running backs on their 53-man roster, but they will have to decide how many wide receivers to keep beyond Nacua, Adams and Atwell, with Xavier Smith and Jordan Whittington filling special teams roles and sixth-round rookie CJ Daniels enjoying a busy training camp and preseason.

Thursday night’s matchup between the Las Vegas Raiders and San Francisco 49ers might have less juice than the one coming two months from now. The Raiders’ former cross-city rivals visit Allegiant Stadium for the fourth consecutive preseason, the final exhibition game for both teams. On Nov. 8, the foes will meet again when Las Vegas returns to the Bay Area for the first time in the regular season since the franchise’s relocation from Oakland.
That resumption of the Battle of the Bay will be rife with drama, but there are also high stakes Thursday night — for specific players. While many Raiders have already solidified their spots on the 53-man roster ahead of Sunday’s roster cutdown deadline, a few competitions remain unresolved. Thursday’s performances will be a factor in the coaching staff’s final decisions.
“These game reps are the most valuable ones that we can use,” Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said. “It’s very helpful (for evaluating) many guys.”
As the Raiders line it up one last time before the games count, here are the players with the most to gain — and the most to lose — in the preseason finale.
Powers-Johnson and Rogers are both going to make the roster. But Thursday will be a pivotal game in their battle for the starting role at right guard.
“This game will be really important for that battle,” Kubiak said. “I know both those guys are going to play this year. We’re counting on both of them, as well as a lot of other guys. So, this competition has only made them better and our team better.”
Powers-Johnson began training camp as the sole right guard working with the starters. But after the first few practices, Rogers began rotating in with the ones. That has continued throughout training camp and the preseason.
Powers-Johnson appears to have a slight advantage in the competition. He was in for presumed starting quarterback Kirk Cousins’ lone drive in the preseason opener, and he’s usually the first guard out there in practices. He was also the Week 1 starter at right guard last season. But the Raiders are pleased with Rogers’ development going into his second season, with coaches complimenting his preparation.
“He has all the talent that you’re looking for,” Kubiak said of Rogers. “We’ve just got to keep getting him better. I like how he works, like the kind of teammate that he is, and he has a bright future ahead of him.”
Both guards figure to get solid work Thursday against the 49ers. And while one will effectively be slotted as the starter ahead of the opener against the Miami Dolphins, expect the competition to continue throughout the season.
The Raiders have a concrete top four at the edge position with Maxx Crosby, Kwity Paye, Malcolm Koonce and rookie Keyron Crawford. But a fifth spot is likely up for grabs, and with Brennan Jackson going on season-ending injured reserve, Slone and Johnson are evidently vying for it.
Slone has impressed the staff since signing as an undrafted free agent in the spring. He’s gotten to work with the second unit frequently in practices, and he had a strong preseason debut against the Arizona Cardinals, notching a sack and three total tackles.
“His disposition is relentless,” defensive line coach Travis Smith said of Slone. “His physicality shows up day in and day out, whether it’s setting edges or it’s rushing with power or converting with a little bit of speed.”
Johnson signed with the team at the start of training camp after spending parts of the last five seasons on the Philadelphia Eagles and New York Giants. It took Johnson extra effort to get up to speed, but he has excelled in his preseason opportunities, earning sacks in both games.
“(He’s a) very instinctive player,” defensive coordinator Rob Leonard said of Johnson. “Tough, very smart. I think his play speaks for itself.”
Both Slone and Johnson can continue to make their case for a roster spot with strong preseason finales. Special-teams opportunities are also key, as each will have to show value there.
Like edge, the Raiders’ receiver position has a steady top four in Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor, Jack Bech and rookie Malik Benson. Dont’e Thornton Jr. figured to be the fifth guy in the mix, but an injury that held him out of preseason action makes him a potential cut or IR candidate. That leaves the door open for one — or maybe two — of Young, Johnson and Thompkins to make the roster.
Young is squarely in position to earn a spot, given his experience playing for Kubiak and special-teams value. The Raiders signed the veteran receiver this offseason after he played four years in Seattle, his last with Kubiak as his offensive coordinator. While Young has just four career catches, he has 697 special-teams snaps under his belt and has been a key figure in coordinator Joe DeCamillis’ units so far. A good preseason finale could earn him more of a shot on offense.
Johnson and Thompkins were signed at the start of training camp as well, putting them behind veterans Shedrick Jackson and Phillip Dorsett and even undrafted free agents Chase Roberts and E.J. Williams Jr. But Johnson and Thompkins have been among the top playmakers with the twos in practice, and Johnson’s 33-yard catch set up the game-winning score in the preseason win over the Houston Texans.
A big play or two from Johnson or Thompkins against the 49ers could make Kubiak and his staff think a bit harder about their standing.
Meredith started 11 games for the Raiders last year, but as the preseason has worn on, he’s tumbled down the depth chart. The veteran served as rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza’s center with the twos to begin training camp. But after a few practices, the Raiders moved third-round rookie Trey Zuhn III into that position, pushing Meredith to second-team left guard and third-team center. Meredith did serve as the second-team center in both preseason games, with Zuhn playing right tackle. But after returning from Houston, Zuhn has moved back to center, and Meredith has been rotating with Atonio Mafi at left guard with the twos.
Meredith’s positional versatility and experience on the left side give him value, but he’ll likely have to show something Thursday to earn a depth spot.
Vance is another player who seems to have fallen out of favor. The second-year defensive back served as the Raiders’ second-team nickel through the start of training camp and the first preseason game. He gave up some big passing plays against the Cardinals and wasn’t much of a factor in the run game, leading Las Vegas to make some changes.
The Raiders mixed Treydan Stukes, Dalton Johnson and Tristin McCollum in at nickel against the Texans, eating into Vance’s reps. In the practices since, Johnson, the fifth-round rookie, has been the first nickel working with the twos, leaving Vance to rotate in afterward.
Johnson appears to be trending toward a roster spot. With his opportunities in Thursday’s game, Vance will have to improve to claim one of the last spots on the team.
Thursday will be just the second game action Richardson sees, as he missed the preseason opener for the birth of his child. The limited snaps make his performance against the 49ers even more important.
Richardson worked primarily with the twos during training camp and looked solid, playing tight coverage and posting a few pass breakups in practices. But he’s been relegated behind rookies Hezekiah Masses and Jermod McCoy in recent practices, both of whom seem to have locked-in spots behind Eric Stokes and Darien Porter.
Richardson would be the team’s fifth corner, and it’s plausible he’s battling with Vance across positions for a roster spot. Their performance — and the team’s preference for where they want more depth — could determine the final cuts.

The Los Angeles Rams aren’t done with Tutu Atwell after all. They have acquired their former wide receiver in a trade with the Miami Dolphins in exchange for running back Jarquez Hunter, the team announced on Thursday.
The Rams are bringing back a receiver they drafted in the second round in 2021 who spent the past five seasons with the team. Atwell was a steady producer from 2022 to 2024, catching 99 passes for 1,343 yards and four touchdowns, and Los Angeles re-signed him last offseason to a one-year, $10 million deal.
However, Atwell fell out of the rotation quickly and finished with just six catches for 192 yards and a touchdown on 15 targets. He was often a healthy scratch down the stretch of the season as the Rams leaned into three-tight end sets and had to fix their special teams units on the fly — and Atwell didn’t contribute to that phase.
But now, the Rams are bringing Atwell back. They feel better about their special teams numbers and are still searching for a dependable No. 3 receiver behind Puka Nacua and Davante Adams.
Hunter was a fourth-round pick in 2025, but he was pushed out of playing time by the steady presence of Kyren Williams and Blake Corum, as well as Ronnie Rivers, who contributes on special teams.
The Rams will take on $1.075 million of Atwell’s contract for this season, marking a difference of nearly $9 million from what they paid him last year. They will incur a cap hit of around $250,000 from Hunter’s deal as part of the trade.
The Rams are now likely to keep just three running backs on their 53-man roster, but they will have to decide how many wide receivers to keep beyond Nacua, Adams and Atwell, with Xavier Smith and Jordan Whittington filling special teams roles and sixth-round rookie CJ Daniels enjoying a busy training camp and preseason.
