full_text:
Vikings rookie safety Jacob Thomas has always been a long shot. Now, he's in line to make the team's 53-man roster. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Tai Felton demanded I go find this play. Scour the internet, he said. The highlight is there somewhere.
And if it doesn’t come up via search? If it’s not easily accessible?
“I will text it to you,” the Minnesota Vikings’ second-year receiver said after one recent practice. “You have to see it.”
As it turns out, the play not only exists, but it’s everywhere. Social media feeds offer all different angles. A “SportsCenter” link still lives online with the following headline: This is the one-handed, state-title-winning TD grab you have to see.
When you press play on the clip , the commentator provides some background. It’s overtime. Stone Bridge High School, a powerhouse program in Ashburn, Va., is facing third-and-16 near the red zone with the Class 5 state championship on the line. The quarterback, Billy Wiles, catches the shotgun snap and looks as if he’s running a sweep to the right. He’s not. Instead, Wiles stops and does what most coaches tell young quarterbacks never to do. He launches a pass across his body.
The football leaves the frame, and then, at the last second, drops from the sky. The receiver underneath the ball, identified as Jacob Thomas, leaps backward, extends his right arm and palms the pigskin with a striking smoothness. The reception sends the sideline into a tizzy. Teammates and coaches are running, jumping, screaming and celebrating. That includes Felton, Thomas’ high school teammate, whose torn ACL paved the way for Thomas to play receiver.
“He was such a baller even back then,” Felton said. “So, yeah, I definitely knew what (the Vikings) were getting.”
Felton believed what almost anyone who has spent meaningful time around Thomas believed: that he would make the Vikings look smart when they signed him as an undrafted free agent this spring.
In fact, many of Thomas’ former coaches begged their scouting friends to take the converted safety late in the NFL Draft. Ironically, according to several of these former coaches, the Green Bay Packers were one of the teams closest to pulling the trigger.
“To be honest,” former James Madison coach Bob Chesney said, “I was a little bit shocked to see some of the guys who went above him.”
“I think it’s silly,” Colin Hitschler, Thomas’ defensive coordinator at James Madison, added. “NFL teams sometimes waste their picks on these elite testers, and here are these elite football players who end up making the team.”
Thomas’ signing as an undrafted free agent came with little fanfare. But even at the time, one NFC executive, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak openly about another team’s roster, pinpointed Thomas as a hidden gem.
Months later, Thomas’ training camp performance is more than just a fun story. It’s an essential development for a Vikings roster lacking rangy safety options with the aptitude to operate the controls of defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ scheme.
After Saturday’s preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens, head coach Kevin O’Connell highlighted Thomas’ intelligence. Flores continued with the compliments Tuesday. The lofty recognition, paired with Thomas’ on-field consistency, brings the details of a revealing journey to the forefront.
For multiple reasons, perplexing as they are, doubt surrounded Thomas at almost every turn.
“It’s the one constant for him,” Hitschler said. “All he does is prove people wrong with a zen and peaceful mentality. He doesn’t wear the chip on his shoulder. He’s not grumpy. It’s just this quiet, internal thing.”
Not even his eye-popping catch earned him a scholarship offer from an FBS school. He attended camps. He contacted coaches. Nothing worked.
Originally, Thomas agreed to play quarterback at the University of Richmond. Miscommunications with the coaching staff gave him second thoughts. Within minutes of publicly announcing his decommitment, then-unheralded James Madison coach Curt Cignetti sent Thomas a direct message.
“Cignetti tells Jacob, ‘I don’t have any scholarships, but I’d love to have you as a walk-on here,’” Thomas’ father, Richard, said. “He came back and told me (and his mother, Geraldine), and we said, ‘Look, if you want to do this, follow your dream.’”
To support Thomas’ decision, Richard, a special agent at the Pentagon, worked an extra 16 hours on Saturdays.
“We just wanted him to accomplish all of the things he wanted in life,” Geraldine added. “Our whole thought has been: How can we do what we have to do to make sure he has a better life than we have?”
Once Thomas arrived on campus, James Madison coaches realized that he was quicker on the field than any stopwatch suggested. He identified formations and deciphered passing concepts. He understood space and angles, almost as if his brain was calculating the picture in front of him with a new-generation operating system.
Perhaps Thomas’ experience as a basketball point guard developed a mechanism for faster reactions. Richard wondered if his years of playing soccer helped, too. Whatever the influence, this skill created opportunity. In 2022, Thomas contributed on special teams. In 2023, he got defensive snaps as a boundary safety. Neither compelled Cignetti to put Thomas on scholarship, a factor in Thomas’ eventual choice to stay at JMU to play for the newly hired Chesney.
The new staff marveled at Thomas’ acumen. Frequently, when he returned to the sideline, safeties coach Anthony DiMichele would ask him about the previous play. Thomas described player positioning in a way that made the coach wonder if Thomas had a photographic memory.
Power 5 programs, including Indiana, attempted to pluck Thomas for massive dollar amounts after his productive 2024 season, but he declined. Loyalty to Chesney and proximity to his family kept him in purple.
Somehow, Thomas’ major role in James Madison’s path to the College Football Playoff still didn’t earn him an invite to the NFL Scouting Combine. Overlooking him — again — would make more sense if he didn’t run a 4.44 40-yard dash at his pro day.
“I think some teams think, ‘If the players at that level are actually good, they’ll portal up,’” Nathan Applebaum, James Madison’s former director of player personnel, said. “But there are exceptions. I told every scout who came into our building that they wouldn’t regret drafting this kid. He’s just so instinctive.”
Vikings scout Michelle Mankoff listened. Her persistence, combined with discussions Vikings staffers had with Thomas to outline how they envisioned him in this defense, piqued his interest. Flores’ philosophy of playing the best players, regardless of draft position or hype, made Thomas’ selection easier.
Quietly this spring, coaches mixed him in with the backups. His ability to handle the communicative aspects of Flores’ scheme — coupled with the hazy status of Harrison Smith and the Vikings safety position — put him even more on the staff’s radar. As is his custom, Thomas succeeded early in training camp and established enough trust to be in line to make the 53-man roster.
He effectively fills gaps against the run. He tracks passes in the deep parts of the field. He does so many of the things he has always done.
This is not revisionist history, either. The proof and the talent, Felton reiterates, is still evident for anyone curious enough to look.

full_text:
Quarterback Drake Maye looks to build off of his stellar sophomore effort. Kevin C. Cox / Getty Images
An intense, eventful offseason gives way to the quest for ring No. 7. The New England Patriots are back in business, taking the highest of hopes into their 2026 campaign.
Last year’s group was a total revelation. New England went 14-3 and cruised through its conference. In just his second season, Drake Maye earned All-Pro votes and MVP runner-up recognition. The Patriots paced the NFL in yardage differential en route to the franchise’s 12th Super Bowl appearance. Despite that deflating loss at the mountaintop, this upcoming season positions the team as week-to-week must-see TV.
There’s a national fixation around head coach Mike Vrabel, who resumes his post after a stunning scandal . There’s massive buzz around newly acquired — and always outspoken — A.J. Brown as he lines up out wide. Maye starts his age-24 season on the MVP shortlist. New England stars in the primetime season opener, a Super Bowl rematch versus the Seattle Seahawks. And the players stamp their passports with a midseason Munich showcase against the Detroit Lions.
The Patriots feel unmissable, but accessing their games is harder than ever amid broadcast changes and streaming exclusives. Here’s your consolidated guide to all 17 regular-season dates. Be sure to follow the Patriots on The Athletic. Senior writer and New Hampshire native Chad Graff has been on the beat since 2022.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Patriots GOAT Tom Brady — he’ll return to Foxborough in Week 9 when New England hosts the Green Bay Packers. Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen, and Amin is partnered with newcomer and recent Hall of Fame inductee Drew Brees. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with the Patriots-Seahawks clash on a Wednesday night. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game and Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from longtime Patriots coach Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the studio personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.
NFL Network has five of the international games, plus a pair of Saturday matchups in Week 16 to be revealed at least two…

As an organizat
full_text:
New York Giants linebacker Arvell Reese and New York Jets edge rusher David Bailey were both top-five picks in the 2026 NFL Draft. Seth Wenig and Scott Boehm / Associated Press
The debate raged throughout draft season, carried into the preseason, and if all goes according to plan, will continue for the next decade. The New York Jets had the No. 2 overall pick ahead of April’s NFL Draft, and it became clear their choice would come down to two players: Arvell Reese and David Bailey
As an organization, they hadn’t decided who they were going to pick until close to draft day.
On one hand, there was Reese, a freak athlete with untapped potential as an edge rusher and the potential to be used as a Swiss Army knife in the new defense Aaron Glenn was building after taking over as play caller this offseason.
On the other hand, there was Bailey, a pure edge rusher with a ridiculous get-off, size, length and athleticism, as well as proven pass rush production at Texas Tech, where he managed 14.5 sacks and 19.5 tackles for loss as a senior.
Likely to be a versatile NFL starter: quick-twitch, disruptive, powerful and explosive.
The common refrain was that in Bailey, the Jets would be getting a sure thing. In Reese, they’d be adding a prospect with a higher ceiling but greater room for error. Nobody — including the Giants, picking at No. 5 — really knew what the Jets were going to do until the pick was announced. The Giants weren’t operating under the assumption Reese would be an option for them; they hadn’t even really considered that he’d make it beyond the Jets at No. 2 or the Titans at No. 4.
And then the Jets picked Bailey. And Reese fell to the Giants.
A versatile defender who has the physical traits to become a dominant pass rusher.
And so now and forevermore, the two will be connected. They will be compared for as long as one or both remain in New York uniforms — this is especially true for Bailey, because the Jets had the option to select either.
On Friday, if both rookies play, they’ll face off on opposite sidelines for the first time in the preseason finale at MetLife Stadium, the home they’ll now share. The comparisons will be hard to escape — almost as hard as it is for quarterbacks to escape them when they are in pursuit.
“Those are two really, really good players, and they’re going to be really good players in this league,” Glenn said on Monday. “The thing is, we wanted to make sure we made the best decision for us going forward, and we felt like Bailey was the best decision. Arvell is a special, special player, and he’s going to do special things in this league — but we like the direction that we went.”
Did the Jets make the right choice?
We won’t know the answer to that for at least a few more years. But that won’t stop anyone from pitting the two against each other along the way.
To help forecast what’s to come, our Jets beat writer (Zack Rosenblatt) and one of our Giants beat writers (Charlotte Carroll) came together to dive into how the Jets and Giants landed on Bailey and Reese as their top selections, how they fit, how they’ve looked so far and what’s to expect in their debut seasons.
Bailey: The Jets didn’t spend as much time in person with Bailey as they did with Reese during the pre-draft process. The Jets even canceled their pre-draft visit with Bailey. Clearly, that was because they were more comfortable with Bailey based on the conversations they’d had with him at the combine and at his pro day. To Glenn and general manager Darren Mougey, Bailey felt like a cleaner fit for the defense. They desperately needed an edge rusher capable of contributing right away, and Reese was viewed as more of a project in that area. In the Jets’ 3-4 base defense, Bailey slots in perfectly as an outside linebacker, and if Reese’s best fit is at off-ball linebacker, where he’ll play for the Giants, the Jets already have Demario Davis and Jamien Sherwood to hold down the fort in 2026. — Rosenblatt
Reese: When it came to all my mock drafts and big boards, I rarely linked the Giants with Reese, simply because I didn’t think he’d be available at No. 5. But with Reese still on the board, the Giants selected their highest-rated non-quarterback in the draft, and in doing so, added an explosive and powerful player to their defense. Reese’s versatility was a big factor for the Giants, who on draft night vowed to find creative ways to deploy their dynamic new defender. While some analysts expected Reese to go play off the edge once he got to the NFL, the Giants immediately said they intended to keep him as an inside linebacker, while finding ways to capitalize on his pass rush potential. — Carroll
Bailey: There’s a legitimate case to be made that no Jets defender, veterans included, has looked better in training camp than Bailey. No one has dominated practices to the degree that Bailey has already managed. In the second practice of camp, Bailey had a rep where he bull-rushed right tackle Armand Membou and running back Breece Hall and got to QB Geno Smith for a sack — one of three that day, plus two tackles for loss.
He’s won some battles with Membou and gotten the better of left tackle Olu Fashanu, too. He also overwhelmed Buccaneers right tackle Luke Goedeke in joint practices with Tampa. Some of his sacks happen so fast that the offensive line and Smith don’t even have time to react. He also tallied a sack against the Steelers in last week’s preseason game. Perhaps most importantly: He’s flashed against the run too, the biggest knock against him coming out of Texas Tech. — Rosenblatt
first of many for the No. 2 pick
📺: #NYJvsPIT on @NFLonCBS , @paramountplus pic.twitter.com/P6yF0fjJZ5
— New York Jets (@nyjets) August 21, 2026
Reese: The 6-foot-4, 243-pound Reese impressed from the start in camp, consistently using speed and power to overwhelm offensive linemen and blow up plays in the backfield during his first week in West Virginia. He hasn’t really slowed down since. He’s also proven effective in pass defense, as he’s been batting away a handful of passes and tallied an interception during camp. It’s a cliché, but he already looks (and carries himself) like an NFL veteran. It might be what you expect from the No. 5 overall pick, but Reese has strung together so many impressive moments and performances throughout camp that there’s little doubt he’s ready to make a big impact his rookie season — Carroll
Bailey: As mentioned, he fits perfectly as an outside linebacker. Bailey seems to be at his best when he rushes standing up, but he’s perfectly capable of putting his hand in the dirt or rushing from the inside, too. It would be a surprise if Bailey didn’t wind up leading Jets edge rushers in snaps, though the bulk of his playing time will come on passing downs. Interestingly, the Jets have dropped both Bailey and Will McDonald into coverage at times, including against the Steelers. Bailey, McDonald and free agent additions Kingsley Enagbare and Joe Ossai form one of the better rotations the Jets have had at the position in a few years. — Rosenblatt
Reese: Reese can do everything, so Giants fans should expect him to get some opportunities to rush the passer off the edge alongside Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux. But as planned, he’s taken most of his snaps this summer at inside linebacker alongside the 6-foot-4 Tremaine Edmunds, with whom he’s already forged a bond.
“There’s never a play where we just line up, and then we just go through the play and then talk after the play,” Reese told The Athletic’s Dan Duggan recently. “We always say something before the play; we damn near say something during the play.”

A.J. Epenesa succumbed to the instinct limned by poets, painters and pillars of salt.
He looked back. The Philadelphia Eagles edge rusher could not resist. For six years, he’d fixed his eyes on the quarterback. For 1,725 previous snaps, including the preseason and postseason, he’d burst into the backfield as a pass rusher.
That’s where the act
full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles hope A.J. Epenesa can boost the team's depth at edge rusher for the first quarter of the 2026 season. Kara Durrette / Getty Images
A.J. Epenesa succumbed to the instinct limned by poets, painters and pillars of salt.
He looked back. The Philadelphia Eagles edge rusher could not resist. For six years, he’d fixed his eyes on the quarterback. For 1,725 previous snaps, including the preseason and postseason, he’d burst into the backfield as a pass rusher.
That’s where the action is, isn’t it?
Surely, he could keep pace in pass coverage with a tight end’s wheel route and risk a peek…
The ball had already left Tyler Huntley’s hand. The backup Baltimore Ravens quarterback had chosen his matchup. And Epenesa was sprinting to catch up as he had never done before — looking back all the while, looking back at the ball. When Epenesa leapt, the pass nearly clipped his outstretched left hand. The ball nestled into Matthew Hibner’s gloves for a 29-yard gain.
Days later, as Epenesa reflected on that pass in the preseason opener, he recalled he wasn’t “too far off” from making a play but could “make that tighter.” He’d learned to not look at the quarterback, to keep his eyes “on the work” — in this case, his coverage.
These are new lessons for a former Iowa defensive lineman — the son of a former Iowa defensive lineman — who, at 270 pounds as an All-American high schooler and at 280 pounds as an All-Big Ten Hawkeye, has known little else than surging across the line of scrimmage.
“I wasn’t covering any wheel routes back then,” Epenesa laughed.
Nor in Buffalo, where Epenesa spent six seasons within former Bills coach Sean McDermott’s attack-oriented, one-gap scheme. Epenesa averaged 0.7 coverage snaps across 105 regular-season and playoff games, according to TruMedia. He totaled four interceptions, including a pick-six in 2023, but he pointed out that each pick was a heads-up play in a series of rushes that forced quarterbacks to make bad decisions.
“I’m kind of put in a different situation now where I won’t be able to get up the field as quickly as I have in the past,” Epenesa said.
Epenesa is a standing edge defender now — a new role, he said, in which he could be dropping in coverage “every other play.” He is covering wheel routes. And the flats in zone coverage. And a list of other dropback responsibilities. He is the latest of a long list of edge rushers who have had to learn how to drop in coverage under defensive coordinator Vic Fangio.
“He’s done really well with it,” Fangio said of Epenesa. “And I think he’ll continue to improve.”
Fangio, who arrived in Philadelphia in 2024, has not considered an edge rusher’s lack of experience in coverage a disqualifying factor. It has been the norm. Former edge rusher Josh Sweat’s coverage snaps per game tripled under Fangio. Nolan Smith’s coverage snaps per game have doubled from his rookie season under former defensive coordinator Sean Desai. That former edge rusher Bryce Huff totaled just eight coverage snaps in the 14 games preceding his departure underlines how Fangio values a player’s skillset and willingness — not his history.
“I believe they wouldn’t have me here if they didn’t think I could do what the whole job entails,” Epenesa said.
Convention has not curbed creativity where Fangio’s influence and the Eagles’ scouting department merge. Zack Baun is the epitome; the reserve-turned-All-Pro had never played inside linebacker before Fangio enlisted him there in 2024. Cooper DeJean, an outside cornerback in college, flourished at nickel last season while doubling as a cornerback in base packages, and will this season double at safety — a position he had never played.
Epenesa initially seemed bound for yet another one-gap system. In March, he reached an agreement with the Cleveland Browns on a one-year deal worth up to $5 million, but the Browns backed out after Epenesa underwent his physical. When asked what happened, Epenesa said, “It was a weird situation,” and “I’ll just leave that in the past and be happy that I’m not a Brown and I’m an Eagle.”
“(I’m) very healthy,” Epenesa added. “Feeling good. And happy to be here.”
Fangio admitted he “didn’t really have any” impressions of Epenesa before the Eagles signed him to a one-year, $1.4 million contract in early June.
Internally, the Eagles viewed Epenesa as a possible fit for the depth they’d struggled to secure in 2025. (Za’Darius Smith, who suddenly retired in October and later signed with the Atlanta Falcons, told reporters Wednesday that he retired because his mother, father and grandmother all died near the same time.) Jaelan Phillips, a midseason trade acquisition, signed a four-year, $120 million deal with the Carolina Panthers. The contracts of an aging or oft-injured collection of veterans — Brandon Graham, Patrick Johnson, Ogbo Okoronkwo, Azeez Ojulari, Joshua Uche — also expired.
The revamped Eagles’ edge rusher room represents somewhat of a motley crew, particularly when it comes to pass coverage. Epenesa is learning an entirely new position. Josh Weru, a former Kenyan rugby player, is learning an entirely new sport. The group’s marquee member, Jonathan Greenard, rarely dropped into coverage before his two-year tenure with the Minnesota Vikings, and, even then, wasn’t asked to cover wheel routes.
Even Arnold Ebekitie, whose 2.7 coverage snaps per game are the most of any Eagles edge rusher, said he needed time to get comfortable in Fangio’s scheme.
The group is green — but supportive. Fangio, too. At the start of training camp, Fangio said he told Epenesa in front of the whole team that the 27-year-old “did a nice job” in practice “for a guy that’s being asked to do a few things that he’s never done before.” It’s notable that Fangio, a blunt and straight shooter with reporters, called Epenesa’s wheel route “a great learning experience.” Fangio was “really happy that happened” because, 1) it took place in a preseason game, which exists to supply such lessons, but also 2) it served as a lesson for everyone in the edge rusher room about how to play that coverage.
The players champion each other with a mix of motivation and grace. Smith called it “a collaborative thing” where they “talk all over” everything. The culture even emboldened Weru, who spent OTAs in Philadelphia before Epenesa’s arrival, to share what he knew with Epenesa.
“This has definitely been a challenge,” Epenesa said. “But the guys I’ve been surrounded with have made this into a really fun endeavor. They’ve made this challenge become more enjoyable. I like challenging myself. But I’m going to mess some things up. And knowing the world isn’t falling apart just because A.J. messed something up — everyone’s been very helpful, encouraging — that’s honestly what’s been helping propel me forward in this situation is having these guys around me.”
Epenesa and the rest of the edge rushers have one final preseason game against the Cincinnati Bengals on Friday night before the Eagles must trim their roster to 53 players by Sunday’s league-wide 6 p.m. ET deadline.
Depth at edge rusher will be critical. Greenard has missed the entirety of training camp after injuring his pectoral muscle while lifting weights during the summer and may not be available for the start of the season. Fangio may call upon a first-timer like Epenesa to fill in a meaningful percentage of snaps. And in this move of confidence, Fangio may receive it back.
“That’s the thing we love about Vic: he’s so constant,” Jalyx Hunt said. “He doesn’t change regardless of who’s in the room. It could be the GM, the head coach, the owner — he’s himself, and he’s confident in what he’s put together. I think he’s put in 40 years, something like that. He’s built his confidence and preparation over 40 years. So, he’s so consistent that whoever’s in the room or whatever position may be open or whoever needs to be called upon in that moment, he’s going to put somebody there he feels he can call upon.”

full_text:
Jonnu Smith was released by the Steelers after one season in Pittsburgh. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
Veteran tight end Jonnu Smith has agreed to a free-agent deal with the Green Bay Packers, a team source confirmed to The Athletic on Thursday. The source spoke on the condition of anonymity because they didn’t have permission to comment publicly.
Smith has spent the past four seasons on four different teams, including the 2025 season with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
Smith was a third-round draft pick of the Tennessee Titans in 2017 and spent his first four seasons there. He signed with the New England Patriots in 2021 and played two years under Bill Belichick before being traded to the Atlanta Falcons. After one year in Atlanta, Smith signed a two-year deal with the Miami Dolphins in 2024 but was traded to the Steelers last offseason.
The Packers are thin on proven options at tight end. Tucker Kraft appears to be fully healthy after rehabbing his torn ACL and is their No. 1. Their No. 2, Luke Musgrave, suffered a neck injury this offseason and hasn’t practiced yet in camp. They also have Josh Whyle, Drake Dabney and Messiah Swinson at the position, but Whyle might be the only one the Packers trust to play significant meaningful snaps in the regular season, and even he doesn’t seem to be much of a threat.
Smith has experience with Packers coach Matt LaFleur, who coached him as the Titans’ offensive coordinator in 2018.
Smith, 31, has been a supplemental part of the passing game for most of his nine-year NFL career. He had one outlier season in 2024, when he set career highs with the Dolphins, catching 88 passes for 884 yards and eight touchdowns. That marks the only time Smith has had more than 50 catches or at least 600 receiving yards in a season.
Smith’s 2025 season was expected to produce better results, because the Steelers’ offensive coordinator was Arthur Smith, who was Smith’s position coach with the Titans and the head coach in Atlanta during Smith’s year with the Falcons. However, the Steelers ended up having more of a tight end-by-committee season, and Smith had just 38 catches for 222 yards and two touchdowns in 17 games.

After weeks of training camp and a pair of preseason games, roster cuts are on the horizon. The initial 53-man roster is due to the league office by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday. The 2025 sixth-ro
full_text:
Eli Heidenreich was the Steelers final draft pick in April. Barry Reeger / Imagn Images
After weeks of training camp and a pair of preseason games, roster cuts are on the horizon. The initial 53-man roster is due to the league office by 6 p.m. ET on Sunday. But before that, several Steelers on the roster’s fringe will have one final chance to make their case, during Thursday’s preseason finale in Buffalo.
Let’s take a look at the players on the bubble with the most on the line.
The 2025 sixth-round pick has always been the key variable in the entire four-QB debate . Howard could have ended the entire discussion by winning the QB2 battle. Instead, given the opportunity to start the second preseason game, Howard threw a pair of interceptions . Will he rebound and prove he absolutely must be on the 53-man roster? Or will another sub-par outing make the Steelers more willing to go the practice-squad route and live with the risks?
Prediction: Keep. The Steelers will hold onto both young QBs, giving themselves two unscratched lottery tickets, as they look ahead to life after Aaron Rodgers.
Moving on from a third-round pick just one year after he was drafted would be a tough look for the Steelers. However, that possibility is looking increasingly likely. Johnson carried the ball just twice for three yards in the first preseason game. He followed that up with 10 carries for 39 yards in the second. Of all the players on the roster, he may be the one who needs an explosive preseason finale to save his roster spot.
Prediction: Cut. The top of the depth chart features a solid one-two punch in Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle. Given the fact that these two backs should eat up the majority of the offensive snaps, the Steelers could lean special teams for the third running back and choose Travis Homer over Johnson.
The Mount Lebanon native produced the feel-good moment of the draft when the Steelers selected him in the seventh round. He was always going to be a long shot to make the team, especially considering they spent a fourth-round pick on return specialist Kaden Wetjen.
Prediction: Cut. Heidenreich is a good candidate for the practice squad. During a developmental season, his best chance of seeing the field will be if Wetjen goes down and the Steelers need a returner. Longer term, the team needs to decide if Heidenreich is a running back or if he needs to transition to wide receiver.
Behind the top two running backs, Nichols is the one who has made the most of his chances. A preseason darling a year ago, he’s picked up where he left off. The question the Steelers have to ask themselves is if they want the RB3 who can contribute more on offense (Nichols) or one with a better track record on special teams (Homer).
Prediction: Cut. Nichols is another good practice-squad candidate. If the Steelers were to sustain an injury to either one of their top backs, it would make sense to elevate Nichols and give him the carries rather than playing Homer on offense.
Reunited with Aaron Rodgers, Tonyan has made a compelling case to stay on the 53-man roster. Of all the players in this story, the 32-year-old tight end has enjoyed one of the best preseasons. He’s caught six passes for 78 yards in the first two preseason games, showing in stadiums what we’ve seen at Saint Vincent College.
Prediction: Keep. Truly, Tonyan is one of the hardest decisions the Steelers will have to make. They’re going to want him to stick around in some way. But will he be a regular enough part of the game plan to keep on the 53-man roster, or is he more Pat Freiermuth insurance that the Steelers can stash on the practice squad? Given Tonyan’s relationship with Rodgers, I’m leaning toward Tonyan making the 53, but I’ve gone back and forth on him a lot. I truly could see it going either way.
McCollum has suited up for 47 NFL games in his career and has made three starts for the Steelers over the last two seasons. He’s been a reliable backup. When you crunch the numbers, he’s one of the players the team probably doesn’t want to cut but might have to.
Prediction: Cut. Brock Hoffman can save the team a roster spot as the primary backup at guard and center. While a numbers crunch could lead the Steelers to cut McCollum, it wouldn’t be surprising to see another team scoop him up for their 53-man roster.
Jones missed about four months in the weight room due to spinal-fusion surgery and it shows. He’s lacking the size and power necessary to play the position at a high level. During the second preseason game, he allowed a pair of sacks.
Prediction: Keep. While his struggles are obvious, I still think he’ll make the team. Jones won’t have to play right away. The Steelers can work on adding some size to his frame over the next couple months. By the time they get to November, if they need to dig into their depth chart, maybe Jones will be up to speed.
The Notre Dame product missed the final six games of the 2025 season due to injury and slid into the sixth round. While he arrived as an unheralded late-round pick, perhaps no other player has done more to boost their stock this preseason. A massive human at 6-5 and 321 pounds, he’s a powerful run stuffer. Rubio has played mostly over the center but has some versatility to line up on the inside shoulder of tackles.
Prediction: Keep. The fans and the media [raises hand] didn’t know a lot about Rubio before training camp. But the Steelers did their homework and found a player worth keeping around.
If you go back to the last preseason game, the 32-year-old Lowry was the first player off the bench in the d-line rotation. He’s played in 132 games with 85 starts and fought back from a 2025 ACL tear in training camp.
Prediction: Cut. While Lowry has been in the league for nearly a decade, the Steelers could choose to go younger on the defensive line. He and Esezi Ottomewo are sitting right on the roster’s fringe. Both would be strong practice-squad players if they aren’t snatched up by another team.
After a gruesome knee injury took away his 2024 season and threatened his career, Holcomb battled back. He added special teams responsibilities to stick around. This offseason, the Steelers signed him to a two-year contract, but moving on would only cost the team $625,000 in dead money.
Prediction: Cut. If the Steelers keep four QBs (one more than last year), six receivers (one more than last year) and all three tight ends (including Tonyan), they have to trim from somewhere. Holcomb is still a player worth keeping on a 53-man roster. But the way Elandon Roberts has come in and made a splash could shake up the depth chart. To me, I think the Steelers can keep either Tonyan or Holcomb, but probably not both.
An undrafted free agent in 2025, Slaughter entered camp buried on the depth chart. However, injuries to Jalen Ramsey and Brandin Echols thrust Slaughter into action with the first-team defense at the “Star” position (nickel corner). He has largely capitalized on his chances, registering six tackles (one for loss) and a PBU in two games.
Prediction: Cut. While Slaughter has played well and another team might be interested in him as a role player, the Steelers already have plenty of depth in Ramsey and Echols.
Though he slipped into the seventh round, Spears-Jennings ran the fastest 40 among safeties at the combine (4.32) and has nearly 6-2 size. He’s been thrust into action with the first-team defense often during camp due to injuries around him. While he may not be ready for the starting lineup yet, he was outstanding as a gunner on special teams and has tangible traits worth developing.
Prediction: Keep. Seventh-round Steelers draft picks are guaranteed little more than a dorm room at Saint Vincent College and a few cafeteria meals. However, Spears-Jennings looks like a player who will stick around.

full_text:
Leonard Williams celebrates with the Lombardi Trophy at the Seahawks' championship parade in February. Jason Redmond / AFP via Getty Images
Seattle Seahawks defensive tackle Leonard Williams is expected to sign a three-year extension, according to a team source who spoke on condition of anonymity because the deal was not yet official.
Williams, who turned 32 in June, was set to enter the final year of a three-year, $64.5 million contract signed in March 2024. A month ago, he said he and the Seahawks had discussed a new contract, and that the sides had time to agree on a deal.
“I’ve had a lot of contracts at this point in my career, and I’ve always noticed players that focus on their contract end up not playing well,” Williams said. “They end up having their head in the wrong place. I’ve noticed that when I focus on being where I’m at, focusing on my team and how I can get better individually, things always tend to work themselves out.”
The 12th-year veteran has had the best stretch of his career since arriving in Seattle via trade from the New York Giants in October 2023. In 2024, he posted 11 sacks and 28 quarterback hits, along with a 92-yard pick six. Williams then earned a second-team All-Pro selection (the first of his career) in 2025 with seven sacks and 22 QB hits in the regular season. He added a sack and three QB hits in the postseason while helping the Seahawks to their second Super Bowl title in franchise history.
Including a franchise tag, this will be Williams’ fifth NFL contract since the New York Jets drafted him with the sixth pick in 2015. He spent five years each with the Jets and Giants and is entering his third full season with Seattle.
The Seahawks also locked up wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba and cornerback Devon Witherspoon earlier this offseason.
It is fairly uncommon for Seahawks general manager John Schneider to sign players over 30 to long-term deals. Throughout his 17-year tenure, Seattle has instead extended the contracts of younger players the team drafted, like Smith-Njigba, Witherspoon and offensive tackle Charles Cross.
But given Williams’ status as one of the team’s leaders, his durability and his production, Schneider determined the USC product was worth making an exception for.
Williams’ contract extension marks the first significant move under the ownership of Vinod and Neeru Khosla. On Wednesday, NFL owners voted unanimously to approve the sale of the Seahawks to the Khosla family for a league-record $9.612 billion.
Shortly after the vote, Vinod Khosla said the family is committed to keeping the Seahawks Super Bowl contenders.
“Our approach is generally going to be long-term focused,” he said. “That’s our inclination always. So keep winning, take a long-term approach, and learn a lot.”
The Seahawks could have another lucrative contract at the position before long. Fellow defensive tackle Byron Murphy II, who tied Williams and Uchenna Nwosu for the team lead in sacks last season with seven of his own, will be eligible for an extension next offseason, after his third year in the NFL.
As a first-round pick (No. 16 in 2024), Murphy’s contract includes a fifth-year option for 2028, and under Schneider’s watch, the Seahawks often wait until a player reaches the final year of his contract before signing an extension. However, Seattle did new deals for 2023 first-round picks Smith-Njigba and Witherspoon.
On Tuesday, Murphy was asked about defensive tackle Jalen Carter resetting the market with his four-year, $152 million contract extension with the Philadelphia Eagles.
“It’s pretty cool to see,” Murphy said. “But I’m not really worried about that right now. Just focusing on me, focusing on what’s happening right now as far as training camp and going into the season.”

summary:

Many key contributors from the Seattle Seahawks’ Super Bowl-winning roster returned ahead of the 2026 season, and coach Mike Macdonald has rested most of them throughout the preseason.
But the Seahawks, who have dropped both exhibition games against the Dallas Cowboys and Tennessee Titans, still have plenty to sort out ahead of their preseas
full_text:
Jalen Milroe, left, should get plenty of reps Friday night, while George Holani is a candidate to be Seattle's top running back. Steven Bisig / Imagn Images
Many key contributors from the Seattle Seahawks’ Super Bowl-winning roster returned ahead of the 2026 season, and coach Mike Macdonald has rested most of them throughout the preseason.
But the Seahawks, who have dropped both exhibition games against the Dallas Cowboys and Tennessee Titans, still have plenty to sort out ahead of their preseason finale Friday night against the Kansas City Chiefs.
Here are five questions the Seahawks can inch closer to answering in Friday’s game, before cutting their roster down to 53 players ahead of Sunday’s 3 p.m. PT deadline.
Who will be Seattle’s No. 1 running back? The picture has yet to crystallize. Meanwhile, much remains up in the air for the Seahawks’ depth players at the position, too.
Jadarian Price, who was drafted in the first round to help replace Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III, has yet to appear in a preseason game and will not play against the Chiefs. He missed time earlier in training camp with what Macdonald described as “upper-leg soreness” but has returned to the practice field as a full participant.
George Holani, who paced the Seahawks with 12 carries for 42 rushing yards against Dallas, could be the No. 1 running back in their season opener on Sept. 9, a Super Bowl rematch against the New England Patriots.
Zach Charbonnet, who led Seattle with 12 rushing touchdowns last season, was placed on the physically unable to perform list before camp and is not practicing, but he is expected to return at some point during the 2026 season. If he remains on the PUP list through Sunday, he will miss at least the first four games of the regular season, but he would not count against the 53-man roster until activated.
Price and Holani are locks to make the 53. Seattle’s third running back spot could still be up for grabs, especially because Emanuel Wilson, who signed in free agency after three seasons with the Green Bay Packers, remains sidelined with a hamstring injury. He could be a candidate for short-term injured reserve, which would keep him out for at least four weeks and save Seattle a roster spot in the meantime.
Jacardia Wright showed off his burst in ripping off a 69-yard touchdown against Tennessee, and Velus Jones Jr. has appeared in both preseason games. If Wilson isn’t ready to go once the regular season gets underway, one of Wright or Jones has an excellent shot to crack the roster.
As for who will be Seattle’s bell cow, it will be between Price and Holani, at least until Charbonnet returns. The Seahawks might rotate the two running backs at the outset, using Price more frequently on early downs and as a receiver and Holani in short-yardage situations and as a pass protector.
Safety Bud Clark will miss the season after being placed on injured reserve Tuesday. He was carted off the field with a broken ankle during Sunday night’s game in Nashville, Tenn.
Clark, 24, was the 64th pick in the 2026 draft out of TCU. He was expected to contribute quickly and compete with Ty Okada to start opposite Julian Love. Instead, Okada is the clear favorite to start next to Love after setting career highs in games started (11) and tackles (65) last season.
Considering both Clark and offseason signee Rodney Thomas II are sidelined, the Seahawks must soon figure out who their top backup safety will be.
Following Sunday’s preseason game, Macdonald highlighted AJ Finley, D’Anthony Bell and Maxen Hook as options to help alleviate the loss of Clark.
Bell, who re-signed with Seattle over the offseason, led all Seahawks defensive backs with four solo tackles (five total) on Sunday. Finley, who is in his third season with Seattle, has three tackles across the two preseason games, while Hook, an undrafted free agent out of Toledo, has seven.
No member of the trio has separated himself yet. Friday is an opportunity to do so.
Injuries have also complicated the Seahawks’ outlook at cornerback. Second-year nickelback Nick Emmanwori had offseason ankle surgery, missing most of training camp before practicing in a limited capacity over the past few days. The Seahawks hope he will be ready for the season opener.
If not, Seattle will have to look elsewhere, especially since the team led the league in percentage of plays with at least five defensive backs on the field last season (92.6), per TruMedia.
Last week, the Seahawks added former Dallas Cowboys cornerback Trevon Diggs on a one-year deal. A two-time Pro Bowler, Diggs is coming off a career-worst season in which he was released by both Dallas and the Green Bay Packers.
Diggs, who has not appeared in a preseason game but will play Friday, could be the front-runner to be the Seahawks’ third cornerback — replacing Riq Woolen, who left in free agency — unless one of the reserves steps up against Kansas City. However, most of his contract is not guaranteed, so nothing is assured.
Veteran Noah Igbinoghene, who signed in free agency, has repped at nickelback throughout camp. So has third-year pro Nehemiah Pritchett, who appeared in every game for the Seahawks last year, including all three playoff contests. Is there room for both on the 53-man roster?
That might depend on the health of third-round rookie Julian Neal, who has not appeared in either preseason game due to a leg injury. If Neal needs more time to recover, he could go on short-term injured reserve, opening up a roster spot. The Seahawks also have a pair of seventh-round rookies, Michael Dansby and Andre Fuller, competing for spots.
Wide receiver Montorie Foster Jr. has been one of the stars of HBO’s “Hard Knocks,” and for good reason. Not only does the 5-foot-11, 188-pound Foster present a compelling case with his blend of agility and catching ability, but he might benefit from the loss of fellow wideout Jake Bobo, who will miss the season with a torn ACL.
Seattle’s top three wide receivers on the depth chart are all but set in stone.
Reigning Offensive Player of the Year Jaxon Smith-Njigba will be around for years to come after signing a four-year, $168.8 million contract extension in March. Former Triple Crown winner Cooper Kupp is back on the scene. The speedy Rashid Shaheed signed a three-year, $51 million contract extension in March as well.
Outside of that trio, though, things get a bit murky.
Tory Horton, who missed most of his 2025 rookie season with a cracked tibia, has not practiced recently due to an undisclosed injury. He could be another candidate for short-term injured reserve. Special teams ace Irv Charles, whom Seattle acquired from the New York Jets in May, has not appeared in either preseason game.
Sixth-round rookie Emmanuel Henderson Jr. has one catch for 7 yards, while 2025 seventh-rounder Ricky White III has hauled in three passes for 26 yards. Seventh-year veteran Cody White, who has the largest frame among Seattle’s receivers at 6-3, 227 pounds, is in his fourth training camp with the franchise after cracking the 53 in 2025.
Given Charles’ absence and the injuries to Bobo and Horton, there are plenty of opportunities to go around. Strong performances by any of Seattle’s reserve wideouts against the Chiefs could go a long way in their bids to make the team.
Entering the preseason, some posited that second-year quarterback Jalen Milroe could supplant veteran Drew Lock as Sam Darnold’s backup. But Milroe has struggled, while Lock has demonstrated he is the clear No. 2 — completing 21 of 27 passes for 143 yards and two touchdowns while repping with the second-team offense this preseason.
Milroe, whom Seattle took in the third round of the 2025 draft, is 11 of 19 for 88 yards with zero touchdowns and two interceptions, both against the Titans. He has been sacked five times. On the positive side, he has rushed six times for 52 yards, something the coaching staff wants him to do more, given his speed.

full_text:
Sam Darnold and Jaxon Smith-Njigba try to defend their title against a stacked NFC. Steph Chambers / Getty Images
There were differences in the details, of course, but the Seattle Seahawks’ 2013 Super Bowl formula was masterfully repurposed for 2025.
Like the Legion of Boom, last season’s “ Dark Side ” defense emerged as an absolute game-wrecker. Like the beloved Marshawn Lynch, Jaxon Smith-Njigba commanded attention and warped opponents as a focal point. Like Russell Wilson, Sam Darnold silenced his many skeptics with efficient, gutsy plat at quarterback. Seattle looked unstoppable with the 12th Man on its side, and the Seahawks lifted the Lombardi Trophy in blowout fashion.
The franchise now has glittering championship rings and new ownership. “Hard Knocks” cameras are in the Seahawks’ faces, while targets are squarely on their backs. Seattle replaces Kenneth Walker III with rookie Jadarian Price in the backfield. And Mike Macdonald’s staff swaps Klint Kubiak for Brian Fleury at offensive coordinator.
Seattle opens the 2026 season on Wednesday, Sept. 9, when it hosts a Super Bowl rematch versus the New England Patriots. It also has a Christmas Day special and several primetime spotlights. Below, we list out the broadcast schedule and network details for all 17 regular-season dates. If you’re not already doing so, be sure to follow the reigning champions on The Athletic , as well as new Seahawks beat writer Andrew Destin .
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
“The NFL Today” pregame show is going to Let Russ Cook . Wilson joins the desk after announcing his retirement in June. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC, and it will air the highly anticipated Christmas night showdown between the Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside one-time Seahawk Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with the Seahawks-Patriots clash on a Wednesday night. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, while another seven — including Seattle’s Week 8 tilt against the Chicago Bears — are exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17.  The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Beast Mode himself to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Legion of Boom luminary Richard Sherman is on the pregame, halftime and postgame shows. Fortunately, Michael Crabtree is not.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.

full_text:
Fourth-round rookie Carver Willis (No. 74) could start for the 49ers at left guard in Week 1. Michael Zagaris / San Francisco 49ers / Getty Images
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — It’s a position that lines up mere feet from the quarterback. It’s one that’s been conspicuous in the San Francisco 49ers’ biggest moments under Kyle Shanahan. And, heading into Thursday’s preseason finale, it’s not resolved.
In fact, you could argue the team is further away from a solution at left guard today, two days after training camp ended and six days before the 49ers board a flight to Australia, than it was when the summer session began a month ago.
The most experienced candidate, Robert Jones, is out with a calf injury, although Shanahan is optimistic Jones will be back at practice next week. Another, Brett Toth, has been dealing with a concussion since early August. And Connor Colby, who seemed comfortably in the lead at the start of training camp, has largely been relegated to the second-team unit in recent weeks. Even Austen Pleasants, who drew more snaps at left guard in recent weeks, is now battling a knee injury.
That’s left Carver Willis, a fourth-round rookie, taking the lion’s share of the first-team repetitions over the past two weeks. Willis is in line to start his second straight preseason game today in Las Vegas.
All the snaps Willis has been getting lately underscore two things:
First, he badly needs them. He played tackle exclusively in college at Washington, and converting to guard in Shanahan’s system is not easy. Colton McKivitz, who was also a college tackle, tried it when he was a rookie in 2020 and was cut the following season. When he returned to the team, it was at tackle, his position ever since.
“It’s extremely hard,” McKivitz said. “I went through it as a rookie, and it didn’t work out for me.”
All the repetitions Willis is getting this close to the season, however, also show how much the 49ers believe in him. His first 11-on-11 snap with the first-string offense two weeks ago was rough. He gave up a sack to defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa and allowed a second one later in that practice.
But he’s improved since, and there’s hope that if he maintains his current trajectory, the 49ers will be able to count on him during the regular season.
“He’s just got to keep getting better every day,” offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. “But I like where he’s at. I like the way he’s working. He’s developing. He’s a young player, and we’ve just got to keep pushing him.”
Outsiders tend to fixate on pass protection when evaluating offensive linemen. The 49ers, however, scrutinize run blocking, especially following a season in which the team’s per-carry average, a robust 4.52 yards in the first eight seasons under Shanahan, dropped to 3.78 yards. It was the first time in his tenure the average fell below 4 yards.
Willis emphasized that the 49ers’ run-blocking scheme is an extremely precise choreography — a Chorus Line but with 315-pound defensive tackles trying to blow up the performance.
His biggest issue right now is that he’s slightly out of step. Or in his words: “My angles in the run game aren’t very complementary of the guys next to me.”
A false step by the left guard on a running play isn’t something a casual observer usually picks up on, but it is obvious — like a sour note during a piano recital — to an expert like offensive line coach Chris Foerster.
“There are so many plays where you can see that the four guys next to me — their hips are on a different angle than mine,” Willis said. “For me right now, it’s studying that aiming point and running on our angles, setting our backside shoulder, all that kind of stuff.”
One benefit to playing left guard for the 49ers, he said, is that he has Trent Williams, who’s played 11,334 career snaps, to his left and Jake Brendel (4,376 career snaps) to the right. And that means he often gets real-time coaching in the huddle.
“Those guys have been so great,” Willis said. “They’ll tell you when you did well. Be like, ‘Hey, great job on that. That’s exactly what we need.’ Or it’s, ‘Hey, come on. You have to see that quicker.’ Or, ‘You’ve got to get hands on the guy.’ I’ve got a combined 23 years of experience next to me. That’s huge. Our vets have been so helpful.”
• Shanahan said there might be “a couple” of Week 1 starters on the field to begin today’s game, but that it will be similar to the preseason opener against Tennessee, when few starters played.
• He said he hopes defensive end Nick Bosa, who hasn’t practiced since Aug. 3 due to knee tendinitis , will practice next week. The team will practice Monday through Wednesday before traveling to Melbourne, Australia, later Wednesday.
• Receivers Mike Evans and Jacob Cowing missed Tuesday’s practice with groin strains. They are on track to return next week, Shanahan said. He gave a similar timetable for quarterback Kurtis Rourke (ribs), cornerback Upton Stout (hip flexor) and Pleasants (knee).
• Offensive tackle Vederian Lowe (high ankle), receiver Christian Kirk (calf) and running back Isaac Guerendo (pectoral) are among the candidates to begin the season on an injury list, like physically unable to perform or injured reserve.

full_text:
Quarterback Jayden Daniels works out during the Washington Commanders' joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens. Stephanie Scarbrough / AP
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — The Washington Commanders’ final preseason game isn’t until Friday night in Baltimore. And while that will be meaningful for down-the-roster players trying to show they deserve an NFL job, the reality is that the bulk of Washington’s training camp concluded with Wednesday’s joint practice against the Ravens.
General manager Adam Peters and his staff have almost all the information they need to construct the 53-man roster and assemble a 17-man practice squad. Final cuts are due by 6 p.m. Sunday, and while the Commanders may well sift through veterans cut by other teams — might a center free up? — the past month has shed light on the team’s strengths, as well as what areas of concern might be paramount for coach Dan Quinn and his staff.
Here’s what we’ve learned since camp began in late July:
That may not be groundbreaking, but after an injury-riddled 2025 season, Daniels returned and had a heck of an offseason — all while adjusting to a new-ish play caller and new scheme. David Blough, his assistant quarterbacks coach the last two seasons, has taken over as offensive coordinator and installed a system that will include parts of what he learned from his time as a quarterback and coach. That means some of what Kevin O’Connell runs in Minnesota, bits of what former Washington coordinator Kliff Kingsbury ran and plenty of what Ben Johnson runs in Chicago (and ran in Detroit).
That’s also meant Daniels preparing to play more under center and make more adjustments at the line — all things that could potentially take time. But Daniels made the transition appear seamless. His command of the system was obvious, and his growth as a leader was unmistakable.
“We track everything,” Blough said earlier in camp. “We’ve tracked every throw he’s made over the last three years. We have metrics to measure all of those statistics. He’s as accurate as he’s ever been. He’s completed as many passes as he ever has. It’s just a testament to asking him to do something different and him wanting to grow and evolve.”
The Commanders decided to cut center Tyler Biadasz in February with a year left on his contract. They had a number of other roster holes to fill in the offseason, but believed upgrading the center position was worth adding to the list. They pursued Tyler Linderbaum, but the Raiders won the bidding with a three-year, $81 million offer, and Washington opted to let its in-house talent compete instead.
That essentially handed the job to Nick Allegretti, a veteran who has played primarily guard. Julian Good-Jones has played only two offensive snaps in his pro career, and Matt Gulbin was drafted in the sixth round out of Michigan State.
How that plan will play out remains a huge question because Allegretti suffered a calf strain on the first day of camp. He returned Aug. 18, but reinjured the calf the following day and hasn’t performed since. In the joint practice against the Ravens, both Gulbin and Good-Jones — who has appeared in one career regular-season game — struggled mightily, contributing to a rough day for Daniels and the offense .
Washington has invested significant capital into its offensive line in recent years, giving right guard Sam Cosmi a contract extension in 2024, then trading for left tackle Laremy Tunsil and drafting right tackle Josh Conerly Jr. in 2025, making it a potential strength coming into the 2026 season.
When Tunsil was lost to a triceps injury , the O-line became cause for concern, yet Brandon Coleman has held up well in his place. The issues, rather, have been inside and due partly to talent and experience, as well as cohesive time together. The Commanders don’t have a clear backup to spell Allegretti, and their depth at guard is thin.
“We need more from us as a group,” Coleman said Wednesday. “O-line-wise, I feel like we got to be the ones to push everything on the offense. I think it was up and down. And that (stuff), we got to obviously correct.”
The rotation with Gulbin and Good-Jones at center, combined with the temporary absence of Cosmi because of an illness, left Daniels working new iterations of the O-line on Wednesday.
“When you don’t get a rep next to somebody the whole camp, and then you end up getting like 12 of them here in joint practice, I mean, it’s like working with new co-workers,” Conerly said.
The Commanders added some depth at tackle by signing veteran D.J. Humphries to a one-year deal on Tuesday. Quinn said Humphries would work mostly at left tackle, with veteran swingman Andrew Wylie remaining as depth on the right side.
“I’m trying to help the team any way I can,” said Humphries, a former Pro Bowler with Arizona who played in just 10 games over the past two seasons with Kansas City and the Los Angeles Rams. “I’m not the savior, though.”
There was a time not too long ago when Washington sorely needed help at receiver. That changed (at least on paper) with the addition of Stefon Diggs . The four-time Pro Bowler agreed to a one-year deal with the Commanders earlier this month, giving them a needed “No. 2” behind Terry McLaurin.
It also created some tough decisions for Peters and Quinn. Rookie Antonio Williams is a lock to make the roster, which leaves eight players — Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffrey, Dyami Brown, Jaylin Lane, Van Jefferson, Jaden Bradley, Nick Nash and Jacoby Jones — vying for the last three or four receiver spots.
Selecting the initial group could come down to their specific skill sets — Brown has rare speed, Lane is the Commanders’ starting punt returner and McCaffrey their starting kick returner, Burks has big-play ability, Jefferson adds size and Bradley has developmental potential — as well their markets. Might Washington try to move anyone on this list? Would they have trade value? And which ones would get claimed by other teams if placed on waivers?
The offensive line wasn’t the only position group to be hit by injuries. The defensive front is dealing with issues large and small.
Tackle Johnny Newton is out indefinitely after tearing a pectoral muscle in the first preseason game against Miami. Outside linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson suffered a knee injury in the joint practice with the Dolphins. Fellow outside backer Odafe Oweh, who signed a four-year deal worth up to $100 million in March, has a strained calf and hasn’t practiced in more than a week. Veteran tackle Tim Settle also missed time because of a calf injury (he returned to practice this week), Daron Payne is sidelined with a lower-body injury, defensive end Drake Jackson was recently placed on injured reserve and Deatrich Wise Jr. has yet to practice since suffering a torn quadriceps last September.
“We play a contact sport, a physical violence sport,” Daniels said Wednesday. “So things are gonna happen. You get put in uncompromising situations where your body’s not really used to. So things happen.”
But the injuries are particularly disruptive for a team trying to learn new systems on both sides of the ball. Blough and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones have not been able to install their schemes with the personnel expected to execute them during the season. Cornerback Trey Amos, expected to be a starter on the outside, returned from a broken leg he suffered last year but sprained his ankle in only his second practice.
“Definitely concerned,” Quinn said of the injuries on Wednesday. “Just don’t like it, and I want to always see the work to make sure their readiness is there. But I’ll assess where it is into next week and then have a better view.”
Washington’s biggest offseason project was transforming the defense, especially its front seven. The additions of Oweh, Chaisson, Charles Omenihu and Settle gave Jones a formidable group on the line, while drafting Sonny Styles in the first round and signing free agent Leo Chenal transformed the linebacking corps.
In the early part of camp…

title: Cardinals QB Update: What We Know About Who Will Play vs. Packers
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are set to play the Green Bay Packers in Friday's preseason finale, setting up one final opportunity for head coach Mike LaFleur and his staff to evaluate who can truly make a difference as roster cuts approach .
All eyes, per usual, are on the quarterback position for the Cardinals. Here's what we know about who is — and isn't — playing in Green Bay:
The Cardinals are not playing most of their starters this week in Green Bay, which would preclude Brissett from playing against the Packers on Friday. Brissett is the established QB1 to begin the season, though all eyes are paying careful attention to how the situation unfolds over the course of the season.
Drawing this back to present day, Brissett and the Cardinals' offense got off to a slow start during joint practice but quickly found their groove against Green Bay , especially at the end of practice.
Prediction: Brissett isn't dressed, alongside a vast majority of starters
Minshew is likely in line to play on Friday as Arizona's effective QB2. With Brissett not dressed, Minshew probably will get a drive or two before the Cardinals shelve him as well.
It's been a fun camp/preseason with Minshew under center, as his willingness to take chances downfield has led to some exciting plays. On the other side of the coin, Minshew is more prone to turnovers.
Early in the regular season, he very well could be the guy to take over if Brissett is forced out of action.
Prediction : Minshew will play a quarter of football before calling it a night at Lambeau Field.
Beck lit the preseason world on fire after his Hall of Fame Game outing, but he hasn't played since. The third-round pick reportedly picked up a ribs injury against Carolina and has been sidelined after trying to push through the pain.
Beck hasn't thrown in any practice over the last week and didn't participate in joint practice festivities against the Packers — which essentially makes him a longshot to play in a live-action game.
Prediction: Beck doesn't play as a precaution for his ribs injury.
We've arrived to the man of the hour.
Slovis is heavily favored to get majority of snaps under center for the Cardinals thanks to Brissett/Beck not playing and Minshew being a high level backup. With Arizona's quarterback room essentially settled, Slovis will be putting on tape for 31 other teams to evaluate this weekend.
The good news? Slovis has performed fairly well in LaFleur's offense this preseason, and that should again be the case.
Prediction: Slovis plays the final three quarters for Arizona, taking over for Minshew.
